status: The 2024 framework of Campanelli–Fiore–Khoshakhlagh (2024), [Witness Encryption for Succinct Functional Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1510), establishes restricted-functionality baselines; broadening expressivity beyond these remains the target.
solved_when: A functional-commitment witness encryption scheme is constructed for a function class strictly beyond NC¹, with explicit quantitative efficiency and assumption bounds.
why: Such a scheme encrypts directly to useful computations on committed data, so wider function classes would make witness encryption usable for realistic computations rather than only the restricted functionalities handled today.
key_works: Campanelli–Fiore–Khoshakhlagh (2024), [Witness Encryption for Succinct Functional Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1510).

title: Sound assignment binding in Groth16-based WE
subfield: Special languages, commitments, and SNARK gadgets
open: Does the encrypted QAP relation in this witness-encryption scheme truly bind every assignment and proof component to the intended statement — even when an adversary supplies malformed inputs? A satisfactory answer establishes binding for all components required by the statement, including malformed-input cases.
status: This is a proposed audit-and-repair target around a 2026 construction; repository issues ([zkenc issue 8](https://github.com/flyinglimao/zkenc/issues/8), [issue 10](https://github.com/flyinglimao/zkenc/issues/10)) are evidence of open questions, not independently reproduced breaks. Key works: Chang et al. (2026), [A Witness Encryption for Quadratic Arithmetic Programs](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8034-7_28).
solved_when: An audit of the construction establishes that the encrypted QAP relation binds all assignments and proof components required by the intended statement, with malformed-input cases handled, and any gaps found are repaired.
why: Without it, an attacker could craft proofs for unintended relations and use them to decrypt ciphertexts, breaking the scheme's security outright.
key_works: Chang et al. (2026), [A Witness Encryption for Quadratic Arithmetic Programs](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8034-7_28); [zkenc issue 8](https://github.com/flyinglimao/zkenc/issues/8); [issue 10](https://github.com/flyinglimao/zkenc/issues/10).

title: Lattice-native WE gadgets
subfield: Special languages, commitments, and SNARK gadgets
open: Can we construct lattice analogues of the useful linearly verifiable SNARK witness-encryption gadgets, under explicit post-quantum assumptions? In other words, can the pairing-oriented gadget framework be rebuilt natively on lattices?
status: The direction is a proposed extension of the pairing-oriented framework of Garg et al. (2025/2026), [A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364); general LWE-based witness encryption remains a separate open line.
solved_when: Explicit constructions of the linearly verifiable SNARK WE gadgets are given from lattice assumptions that are plausibly post-quantum secure, with formal proofs under stated assumptions.
why: It would bring practical special-language conditional encryption toward post-quantum security, whereas the existing gadgets depend on pairings.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025/2026), [A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364).

title: Consistency across heterogeneous WE gadgets
subfield: Special languages, commitments, and SNARK gadgets
open: Can cryptographic gadgets built for different commitment schemes and different verifier equations be composed while guaranteeing they all refer to the same witness, message, and statement? Formally, this asks for a proof of cross-gadget consistency across heterogeneous witness-encryption gadgets in a single composed system.
status: The composition is a proposed target; gadgets that are independently secure need not enforce cross-gadget consistency. Related work includes Garg et al. (2025/2026), [A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364), and Campanelli–Fiore–Khoshakhlagh (2024), [Witness Encryption for Succinct Functional Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1510).
solved_when: A composition method is given that combines gadgets for distinct commitments and verifier equations and proves they refer to the same witness, message, and statement.
why: It enables realistic verifiers assembled from specialized components, rather than requiring a single monolithic gadget.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025/2026), [A Framework for Witness Encryption from Linearly Verifiable SNARKs and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1364); Campanelli–Fiore–Khoshakhlagh (2024), [Witness Encryption for Succinct Functional Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1510).

title: Useful reductions to homogeneous linear equations
subfield: Special languages, commitments, and SNARK gadgets
open: Can the natural conditions arising in applications be efficiently reduced, witness in hand, to the homogeneous-linear-equation relation supported by existing special-language lattice constructions — while preserving the security guarantees of that relation? In other words, which real-world statement languages are usable with extractable witness encryption for homogeneous linear equations?
status: This is a proposed applicability target beyond the 2023 primitive construction of Tran–Vaudenay (2023), [Extractable Witness Encryption for the Homogeneous Linear Equations Problem](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-41326-1_9); no such reductions are yet established.
solved_when: An efficient witness-preserving reduction is given from a concrete class of application conditions to the homogeneous-linear-equation relation, with a proof that the reduction preserves the primitive's security promises.
why: It determines the actual reach of special-language lattice witness encryption: without such reductions, the primitive stays confined to its native equation relation and cannot serve real application conditions.
key_works: Tran–Vaudenay (2023), [Extractable Witness Encryption for the Homogeneous Linear Equations Problem](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-41326-1_9).

title: General witness PRFs below iO
subfield: Witness PRFs and witness maps
open: Can general witness PRFs be built from assumptions substantially weaker than indistinguishability obfuscation — or is there a qualified barrier showing that iO (or something comparably strong) is essentially necessary?
status: Witness PRFs date to Zhandry (2014/2016), [How to Avoid Obfuscation Using Witness PRFs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/301); recent efficient constructions by Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079), address special commitment relations rather than the general case.
solved_when: Either a construction of general witness PRFs from a demonstrably weaker assumption than general iO is given, or a formal separation/barrier result is proved ruling out such constructions under stated qualifications.
why: General witness PRFs would yield reusable public witness-gated evaluation and noninteractive key exchange without the full weight of obfuscation.
key_works: Zhandry (2014/2016), [How to Avoid Obfuscation Using Witness PRFs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/301); Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079).

title: Full security for UP witness PRFs
subfield: Witness PRFs and witness maps
open: Can we achieve the strongest form of adaptive witness PRF security for languages in unambiguous NP (UP), with tight reductions and precisely bounded auxiliary input? In other words, is there a construction whose adaptive security for unique-witness languages matches the best known for general NP, without extra loss?
status: The 2024 UP-SNARK work of Mathialegan–Peters–Vaikuntanathan ([Adaptively Sound Zero-Knowledge SNARKs for UP](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/227)) provides a specialized route toward this goal; its exact guarantees and security losses remain to be worked out.
solved_when: A witness PRF (or equivalent primitive) for UP is proven adaptively secure with a tight reduction and an explicit bound on the auxiliary input, i.e., the guarantees and concrete security losses are fully characterized.
why: A solution exploits the unique-witness structure of UP to get strong adaptive security without inheriting unnecessary general-purpose assumptions, potentially yielding simpler or more efficient primitives than NP-general constructions.
key_works: Mathialagan–Peters–Vaikuntanathan (2024), [Adaptively Sound Zero-Knowledge SNARKs for UP](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/227).

title: Lattice WPRFs for vector openings
subfield: Witness PRFs and witness maps
open: Can we build a weak PRF for vector-commitment openings from standard lattice assumptions, with compact outputs and efficient local evaluation, as a post-quantum analogue of the existing pairing-based construction?
status: The problem is posed as the post-quantum counterpart to the pairing-based construction of Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079); no lattice construction is currently known. Related directions include lattice vector commitments and post-quantum NIKE.
solved_when: A construction exists that (i) rests on standard lattice assumptions, (ii) supports vector-commitment openings, (iii) admits efficient local evaluation, and (iv) comes with a security proof; the target is matching the 2026 pairing-based construction in functionality with quantum-resistant security.
why: Such WPRFs yield quantum-resistant registration procedures and non-interactive asynchronous key establishment, giving a post-quantum replacement for the pairing-based route.
key_works: Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079).

title: Functional vector-opening WPRFs
subfield: Witness PRFs and witness maps
open: Can a witness PRF be evaluated on proofs about functions of committed vectors — not just proofs that locally open a particular position — so that anyone holding a valid witness for such a statement can compute the PRF output with a compact key, and outputs remain consistent across evaluations?
status: This is a proposed expressivity extension of the 2026 vector-opening primitive of Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079).
solved_when: A functional vector-opening WPRF exists in which evaluation is possible from proofs of functions of committed vectors (rather than only local openings), keys are compact, and outputs are consistent; no quantitative budgets beyond these are specified.
why: It would enable policy-based public evaluation over committed datasets, where third parties can derive PRF outputs whenever a committed vector satisfies a stated functional property.
key_works: Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079).

title: Puncturable vector-opening WPRFs
subfield: Witness PRFs and witness maps
open: Can a witness PRF for vector-opening relations be punctured at selected inputs — excluding them from evaluation — without revealing the outputs at those points and without causing the public evaluation key to grow linearly with the size of the punctured domain?
status: This is a proposed synthesis combining puncturable-WPRF applications with recent vector-opening constructions. Key works: Pal–Dutta (2020), [Semi-Adaptively Secure Offline Witness Encryption from Puncturable Witness PRF](https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/479); Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079).
solved_when: A construction of a puncturable vector-opening WPRF is given whose punctured keys both hide the outputs at punctured points and remain sublinear (ideally constant or polylogarithmic) in the number of punctures, with a formal security proof.
why: Such a primitive would enable revocation mechanisms and offline encryption compilers built on witness encryption, removing the need for online interactions when excluding users or inputs.
key_works: Pal–Dutta (2020), [Semi-Adaptively Secure Offline Witness Encryption from Puncturable Witness PRF](https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/479); Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079).

title: Dynamic vector-WPRF updates
subfield: Witness PRFs and witness maps
open: Can a vector-WPRF scheme support updates — to committed vectors and to public WPRF keys — with work sublinear in the vector length, while ensuring that stale openings cannot be used to evaluate outputs of a new epoch that they are not authorized for?
status: The current state of the art is static vector-opening constructions; the dynamic-updates lifecycle is a proposed target beyond them. Key work: Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079). Related lines include dynamic accumulators and updatable commitments.
solved_when: An explicit construction achieves sublinear-work updates of both the committed vector and the public key, with a proof that openings from prior epochs cannot evaluate unauthorized outputs in the updated epoch.
why: It would let witness-PRF-based vector commitments serve changing registries and long-lived applications, rather than only static settings where every change requires re-issuing from scratch.
key_works: Bhadauria et al. (2026), [Witness Pseudorandom Functions for Vector Commitments and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1079).

title: Repair the constrained-WPRF CCA-FE proof
subfield: Witness PRFs and witness maps
open: Does the constrained-WPRF construction of Pal–Dutta actually yield chosen-ciphertext-secure functional encryption as claimed, or does the proof gap break the implication? In particular, can the one-time-pad-related gap in Theorem 3 be repaired, or can the claimed implication be separated from the proposed assumptions?
status: The April 2026 revision of Pal–Dutta (2021, revised 2026), [Chosen Ciphertext Secure Functional Encryption from Constrained Witness PRF](https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/512), explicitly notes a one-time-pad-related gap in Theorem 3; the gap remains open.
solved_when: Either a corrected proof of Theorem 3 closes the identified one-time-pad-related gap, or a separation is shown demonstrating that CCA-secure functional encryption does not follow from the constrained-WPRF assumptions as claimed.
why: It determines whether a claimed downstream primitive — chosen-ciphertext-secure functional encryption — genuinely follows from the proposed constrained-WPRF assumptions, which affects the validity of any further constructions built on this route.
key_works: Pal–Dutta (2021, revised 2026), [Chosen Ciphertext Secure Functional Encryption from Constrained Witness PRF](https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/512).

title: Cross-block function binding
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: When a large plaintext is split into blocks and each block is encrypted independently under a plain witness-encryption application compiler, can we guarantee that all blocks are bound to one consistent function, policy, and output — i.e., that no adversary can make the decrypted blocks correspond to different functions or policies?
status: This is a proposed compositional strengthening of the plain-WE framework of Freitag–Waters–Wu (2023/2025), [How to Use (Plain) Witness Encryption: Registered ABE, Flexible Broadcast, and More](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/812); no construction or proof is known yet.
solved_when: A formal binding notion for cross-block consistency is defined, and the plain-WE application compilers of the 2023/2025 framework are shown (or modified) to satisfy it, ruling out mixed-block attacks.
why: Without such binding, adversaries can mix blocks encrypted under different functions or policies, breaking security of registered and broadcast applications built from plain WE.
key_works: Freitag–Waters–Wu (2023/2025), [How to Use (Plain) Witness Encryption: Registered ABE, Flexible Broadcast, and More](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/812).

title: Rich monotone batch policies from plain WE
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: Can witness encryption, in its plain form plus weaker additions than full indistinguishability obfuscation, support richer classes of monotone policies while keeping batch ciphertexts succinct? Formally, which monotone policy classes beyond the restricted regimes already achievable admit succinct batch witness-encryption schemes without resorting to full iO?
status: Recent constructions exist for CNF/DNF and other restricted regimes; succinctness for broader policy classes remains a distinct, unsolved question. Key work: Devadas–Jain–Waters–Wu (2025/2026), [Succinct Witness Encryption for Batch Languages and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/944).
solved_when: A construction from plain witness encryption (with additions weaker than full iO) is given that supports a broader monotone policy class with succinct batch ciphertexts, where succinctness for such broader policies is shown to be distinct from what current restricted-regime constructions achieve.
why: It would enable compact encoding of conditions that depend on many independent facts at once, something currently out of reach for restricted policy classes.
key_works: Devadas–Jain–Waters–Wu (2025/2026), [Succinct Witness Encryption for Batch Languages and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/944).

title: Heterogeneous succinct batch WE
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: Can a witness encryption scheme batch statements drawn from many different relation families while keeping ciphertext overhead sublinear in the batch size, without requiring a universal verifier whose cost scales with the entire collection of relations? Formally, is there a succinct batched encryption for heterogeneous languages that avoids universal-circuit-style compilation over the full relation set?
status: Currently a proposed extension of the 2025 batch framework of Devadas–Jain–Waters–Wu (2025/2026), [Succinct Witness Encryption for Batch Languages and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/944); related directions include universal circuits and heterogeneous proof aggregation.
solved_when: A construction is given that encrypts to a batch of statements across distinct relation families with ciphertext size sublinear in the batch size, and whose verification cost does not scale with the size of the whole relation collection.
why: Real-world escrow scenarios combine signatures, computations, and commitments in a single batch; a solution would let such mixed escrows be handled succinctly rather than paying universal-verifier overhead.
key_works: Devadas–Jain–Waters–Wu (2025/2026), [Succinct Witness Encryption for Batch Languages and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/944).

title: Succinctness in both batch count and verifier size
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: Can a witness encryption scheme achieve ciphertext size that is simultaneously sublinear in both the number of statements being batched and the size of the verifier's description, under an explicit setup and input-access model? In other words, can succinctness be obtained in both the batch dimension and the verifier-description dimension at once?
status: A stronger succinctness target has been proposed. The state of the art is the work of Devadas–Jain–Waters–Wu (2025/2026), [Succinct Witness Encryption for Batch Languages and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/944).
solved_when: A construction is given whose ciphertext growth is sublinear in the batch size and sublinear in the verifier-description size, with the setup and input-access model made explicit; a matching lower bound would settle the negative direction.
why: Compressing the number of statements does not automatically compress their descriptions, so hidden linear costs can silently dominate in large applications; achieving both would prevent this.
key_works: Devadas–Jain–Waters–Wu (2025/2026), [Succinct Witness Encryption for Batch Languages and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/944).

title: Updatable succinct batch WE
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: Can witness encryption support batched ciphertexts whose defining conditions can evolve over time — adding or removing members of the batch — at update cost sublinear in the batch size, while preserving adaptive security and ensuring that changes made prospectively never alter ciphertexts already copied? Formally, the goal is an updatable succinct batch witness encryption scheme with sublinear-cost updates, adaptive security, and a clean separation between prospective updates and previously derived ciphertexts.
status: Updatable witness encryption exists as of 2025 (Wang–Zhang (2025), [Witness encryption with updatable ciphertexts](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11432-024-4214-0)); combining it with strong batch succinctness remains the open target.
solved_when: A construction is given that supports adding or removing batch conditions with update cost sublinear in the batch size, preserves adaptive security, and provably separates prospective changes from already copied ciphertexts.
why: It would support evolving portfolios and long-lived conditional records, where the access conditions must change over time without re-encrypting everything.
key_works: Wang–Zhang (2025), [Witness encryption with updatable ciphertexts](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11432-024-4214-0).

title: Simultaneously short signature-WE keys and ciphertexts
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: Can signature-based witness encryption be built so that public keys, setup, and ciphertexts are all small at once? More precisely, can expressive schemes achieve short parameters in every component simultaneously, rather than trading a linear cost from ciphertexts into keys or setup?
status: Compact ciphertexts (Avitabile et al. (2024), [Signature-based Witness Encryption with Compact Ciphertext](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1477)) and silent-threshold results (Waters–Wu (2026), [Silent Threshold Cryptography from Pairings: Expressive Policies in the Plain Model](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1547)) provide recent baselines.
solved_when: A construction of expressive signature-based witness encryption is given in which public-key size, setup cost, and ciphertext size are all simultaneously sublinear (or otherwise reduced together), with no component merely absorbing the linear cost displaced from another.
why: It would make event-certificate encryption scalable for systems with many senders and signers.
key_works: Avitabile et al. (2024), [Signature-based Witness Encryption with Compact Ciphertext](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1477); Waters–Wu (2026), [Silent Threshold Cryptography from Pairings: Expressive Policies in the Plain Model](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1547).

title: Adaptive compact signature WE
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: Can witness encryption for signatures be made secure against adaptive corruptions and adaptively chosen statements, without giving up the compact ciphertext and key sizes achieved by recent signature-based constructions? Formally, can adaptive security be attained while preserving the concrete compactness guarantees of the state of the art?
status: The silent-threshold baseline (Waters–Wu (2026), [Silent Threshold Cryptography from Pairings: Expressive Policies in the Plain Model](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1547)) provides specific static and tag-CCA guarantees; these should not be silently upgraded to adaptive ones. Related directions include adaptive threshold cryptography and selective-to-adaptive transformations.
solved_when: A signature-based witness encryption scheme is proven secure under adaptive corruption and adaptive statement adversaries while matching the compactness parameters of the recent signature-WE constructions (including the silent-threshold baseline's static and tag-CCA guarantees strengthened to adaptive analogues).
why: Adaptive security covers evolving committees and adversarially chosen event certificates — the cases that arise in practice once the encrypted event is not fixed in advance.
key_works: Waters–Wu (2026), [Silent Threshold Cryptography from Pairings: Expressive Policies in the Plain Model](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1547).

title: Nonlinear homomorphic signature WE
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: Can signature-based witness encryption support useful nonlinear computations on encrypted data while preserving compactness and security beyond the homomorphic classes already established? Formally, this asks for nonlinear homomorphic evaluation on signature-WE ciphertexts that goes beyond the known homomorphic classes.
status: Pairing, LWE, and Ring-LWE homomorphic baselines already appear in the revised work of Kavousi–Seres (2025/2026), [Homomorphic Signature-based Witness Encryption and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/443).
solved_when: A signature-based witness encryption scheme is constructed that homomorphically supports useful nonlinear computations, with compactness and security beyond the established homomorphic classes.
why: It enables richer private aggregate decisions and conditional computations on encrypted data than currently possible.
key_works: Kavousi–Seres (2025/2026), [Homomorphic Signature-based Witness Encryption and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/443).

title: Autonomous hidden-policy signature WE
subfield: Offline, batched, positional, and signature-based WE
open: Can we build a signature-based witness encryption scheme in which the signing policy stays hidden, ciphertexts remain compact, and decryption happens autonomously — with no online intermediary that must learn or reveal the policy?
status: The separate ingredients exist: statement-oblivious threshold witness encryption (Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668)) and silent threshold cryptography with expressive policies in the plain model (Waters–Wu (2026), [Silent Threshold Cryptography from Pairings: Expressive Policies in the Plain Model](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1547)); combining them remains open.
solved_when: A witness encryption scheme exists that simultaneously hides the signature policy, achieves compact ciphertexts, and enables autonomous release (decryption triggered by a valid signature without any policy-revealing online intermediary).
why: Such a scheme would enable confidential event subscriptions and private release rules, where users can subscribe to encrypted events without the release conditions being exposed.
key_works: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668); Waters–Wu (2026), [Silent Threshold Cryptography from Pairings: Expressive Policies in the Plain Model](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1547).

title: Post-quantum NP-WE from well-studied falsifiable assumptions
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Can we build witness encryption for all NP relations, secure against quantum adversaries, from well-studied falsifiable post-quantum assumptions alone? Formally, the goal is a construction that avoids both idealized obfuscation and newly introduced evasive or hinted assumptions.
status: The problem remains unresolved as of August 2026; it concerns quantum attackers against classical witnesses. Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195), is a key related work.
solved_when: A witness encryption scheme for arbitrary NP relations is constructed, proven post-quantum secure against quantum attackers targeting classical witnesses, and based solely on established falsifiable post-quantum assumptions (no ideal obfuscation, no evasive/hinted assumptions).
why: It would give conditional encryption of ordinary statements a defensible post-quantum foundation.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Plain-model QMA-WE with classical ciphertexts
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Can witness encryption for QMA be built in the plain model with purely classical ciphertexts, under well-studied assumptions — or do substantially broader impossibility results rule it out?
status: Candidate constructions exist only in the oracle model. The August 2026 negative result of Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195), is conditional and restricts the reduction. Earlier, Bartusek–Malavolta (2022), [Indistinguishability Obfuscation of Null Quantum Circuits and Applications](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2022.15), gave related obfuscation-based techniques.
solved_when: An explicit plain-model QMA-WE construction with classical ciphertexts is proved secure under well-studied assumptions, or a substantially unconditional impossibility result is established (going beyond the current conditional restriction on the reduction).
why: A solution would let classical encrypted records be unlocked by quantum evidence alone, giving a post-quantum classical witness-encryption primitive; broader impossibility would likewise delimit what quantum obfuscation can hope to achieve.
key_works: Bartusek–Malavolta (2022), [Indistinguishability Obfuscation of Null Quantum Circuits and Applications](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2022.15); Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Quantum ciphertexts beyond classical-output barriers
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Can witness encryption for QMA be built with genuinely quantum ciphertexts from assumptions weaker than what classical-ciphertext constructions require, and does consuming (destroying) the quantum ciphertext during decryption reduce the cryptographic power needed? The formal goal is a QMA witness-encryption scheme whose ciphertexts are quantum states, based on weaker plain-model assumptions, with an analysis of whether consumable ciphertexts weaken the security or feasibility requirements.
status: The 2026 classical-ciphertext separation (Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195)) leaves this model untouched. Related foundations trace to Alagic–Fefferman (2016), [On Quantum Obfuscation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01771).
solved_when: A construction of QMA witness encryption with quantum ciphertexts is given from weaker plain-model assumptions than classical-ciphertext schemes, together with a determination of whether ciphertext consumption reduces the required cryptographic power.
why: It tests whether physical quantum resources change the feasibility landscape of witness encryption, which classical-output barriers leave unresolved.
key_works: Alagic–Fefferman (2016), [On Quantum Obfuscation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01771); Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: A concrete QMA–QCIP[2] gap assumption
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Can the average-case gap between QMA and QCIP[2] — the separation currently taken as an assumption — be derived from a concrete, recognizable quantum hardness problem, with yes-instances and witnesses that can be generated efficiently?
status: This is an explicit open problem as of August 2026; the separation of Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195), currently assumes this gap rather than deriving it.
solved_when: The QMA–QCIP[2] gap used by the separation is grounded in a concrete quantum hardness assumption, together with efficiently generated yes-instances and witnesses.
why: It grounds the barrier in a recognizable computational problem, replacing an ad hoc assumption with standard hardness.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Adaptive-query QMA-WE separation
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Does the falsifiable-assumption barrier for quantum-witness encryption survive when the reduction is allowed to adapt its later adversary queries based on earlier answers — or can that adaptivity be exploited constructively to bypass the barrier?
status: The August 2026 theorem, due to Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195), excludes adaptive queries.
solved_when: The barrier is extended to reductions that choose later adversary queries from earlier answers, or a constructive use of adaptivity yields a bypass of the barrier.
why: It determines whether adaptivity is a genuine escape route from the impossibility, and thus whether the current form of the barrier is definitive.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Coherent-query QMA-WE separation
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Does the known separation argument still hold when the adversary is granted coherent, superposition access to the challenger rather than only classical queries? Formally, can the barrier be extended to an explicit reversible interface with a specified ancillary-state model?
status: The 2026 theorem of Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195), restricts reductions to classical queries.
solved_when: A theorem (or refutation) is established for reductions making coherent superposition queries under an explicit reversible interface and ancillary-state model, showing the barrier extends to or fails for such quantum adversaries.
why: It tests whether intrinsically quantum reductions evade the known argument, determining whether the separation is a genuine quantum phenomenon or an artifact of classical-query restrictions.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Malformed-ciphertext reductions for QMA-WE
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Can reductions that feed a reduction algorithm malformed or specially correlated ciphertexts establish witness encryption for QMA beyond what honest-ciphertext reductions can achieve? Formally, do such techniques overcome the honest-ciphertext barrier identified for QMA-WE?
status: This is an explicit gap left open by the August 2026 theorem. Related context: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195). Related topics include non-black-box simulation and malformed-query reductions.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) is given that malformed or specially correlated ciphertext reductions can (or cannot) establish QMA-WE beyond the honest-ciphertext barrier, closing the explicit gap in the August 2026 theorem.
why: It determines whether chosen-ciphertext-style techniques offer a positive route to QMA-WE, or whether the barrier rules them out.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Security-parameter-changing QMA-WE reductions
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Can the separation be extended to reductions that query attackers running at different security parameters, while still accounting for the advice, runtime, and success probability of the queries? Formally, this asks whether a parameter-changing (complexity-leveraging) reduction can be ruled out under the same framework, without the assumption that the reduction preserves the security parameter.
status: The 2026 barrier of Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195), assumes parameter preservation; the cross-parameter, nonuniform-advice case remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that no reduction querying attackers across different security parameters — with explicit tracking of advice, runtime, and success — can bypass the separation; equivalently, the 2026 barrier is re-established or broken once parameter preservation is dropped.
why: It determines whether complexity leveraging bypasses the separation result, i.e., whether the barrier against reducing quantum-witness encryption to falsifiable assumptions survives the standard technique of querying attackers at larger security parameters.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Selective-instance QMA-WE foundations
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Can witness encryption for QMA, secure on a per-instance basis, be built from falsifiable assumptions? Alternatively, can the known separation between quantum indistinguishability obfuscation and falsifiable assumptions be extended to instances chosen by the reduction?
status: The 2026 theorem of Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195), addresses an adversary-generated-instance game.
solved_when: A construction of selectively secure per-instance QMA witness encryption is given whose security reduces to a falsifiable assumption, or the separation is extended to cover reduction-chosen instances.
why: It could enable encrypting to fixed high-value quantum conditions while resting on weaker, more standard foundations.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Weaken the separation gap to QMA versus QCMA
subfield: Post-quantum classical WE and quantum-witness encryption
open: Can the known barrier for quantum-witness encryption be derived from an average-case separation between QMA and QCMA alone, or is some stronger interactive gap genuinely necessary to prove it?
status: The current theorem assumes a separation between QMA and QCIP[2]; related work appears in Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).
solved_when: A proof of the encryption barrier is established assuming only an average-case QMA–QCMA gap, or a formal explanation is given of why a stronger interactive separation (such as QMA–QCIP[2]) is required.
why: It would tie the cryptographic barrier to a more familiar quantum complexity distinction, namely quantum versus classical witnesses, rather than to a stronger interactive assumption.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), [Separating Quantum Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Falsifiable Assumptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25195).

title: Quantum-learning characterization of QMA-WE
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can QMA witness encryption (QMA-WE) be characterized by the hardness of learning quantum states, mirroring the classical equivalence between witness encryption and NP-hardness of learning? A satisfactory answer should make the connection concrete through explicit witness-to-decryptor maps and finite-copy access to the quantum witness states.
status: This is a proposed extension of the 2025 classical learning equivalence; key works include Goldberg–Kabanets (2025), [Witness Encryption and NP-Hardness of Learning](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.34), and Alagic–Fefferman (2016), [On Quantum Obfuscation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01771).
solved_when: A characterization of QMA-WE is established via quantum learning hardness, with explicit witness-to-decryptor maps and finite-copy access, in direct analogy to the 2025 classical learning equivalence.
why: A solution would expose new quantum complexity foundations for encryption, extending the classical learning–witness-encryption connection into the quantum setting.
key_works: Goldberg–Kabanets (2025), [Witness Encryption and NP-Hardness of Learning](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2025.34); Alagic–Fefferman (2016), [On Quantum Obfuscation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01771).

title: Transfer from unique quantum witnesses
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can general QMA witness encryption be reduced to the case where the quantum relation has a unique accepting witness? That is, can structured transformations efficiently map any available witness into an isolated accepting space?
status: The uniqueness problem dates to 2008. Recent work — Anshu–Haferkamp–Hwang–Nguyen (2026), [On the Complexity of Unique Quantum Witnesses and Quantum Approximate Counting](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.10) — establishes black-box obstacles alongside qualified positive structure. Related directions include quantum Valiant–Vazirani and the unique local Hamiltonian problem.
solved_when: An efficient transformation is exhibited that reduces general QMA-WE to unique-witness quantum relations, mapping an available witness into the isolated accepting space.
why: It tests whether uniqueness can simplify quantum conditional encryption, potentially turning general witness encryption into a more tractable structured setting.
key_works: Anshu–Haferkamp–Hwang–Nguyen (2026), [On the Complexity of Unique Quantum Witnesses and Quantum Approximate Counting](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.10).

title: QMA(2)-WE with product-witness soundness
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can we build a witness-encryption scheme for a QMA(2) verifier that hides its message whenever no product-form (unentangled) witness makes the verifier accept, even if some entangled witness would? Formally, the encryption should be semantically secure conditioned on the verifier rejecting all product witnesses, so soundness is measured only against the unentangled-witness regime.
status: This is a proposed model at the research frontier; no construction is known. Ordinary QMA witness encryption based on null-circuit obfuscation does not enforce the unentanglement constraint and therefore does not yield product-witness soundness for QMA(2). Related background includes Harrow–Montanaro (2013), [Testing Product States, Quantum Merlin–Arthur Games and Tensor Optimization](https://doi.org/10.1145/2432622.2432625), with related topics QMA(2), separability testing, and tensor optimization.
solved_when: A witness-encryption scheme is constructed whose decryption correctness holds for accepted product witnesses and whose security holds precisely when no accepted product witness exists — even in the presence of entangled witnesses for the underlying verifier.
why: Success would extend conditional encryption from classical NP-style evidence to multiprover quantum evidence, where the natural proof resource is an unentangled product state rather than a single quantum witness.
key_works: Harrow–Montanaro (2013), [Testing Product States, Quantum Merlin–Arthur Games and Tensor Optimization](https://doi.org/10.1145/2432622.2432625).

title: WE for stoquastic witness languages
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can we build an efficient witness encryption scheme for some natural StoqMA-complete or stoquastic-Hamiltonian relation, under assumptions weaker than those needed for general QMA witness encryption? In other words, find a restricted class of stoquastic witness languages for which encryption of the witness is achievable without the full power of QMA-WE.
status: This is a proposed special-language program. It is known that stoquastic structure does not automatically yield a classical witness-encryption construction. Related work includes Cubitt–Montanaro (2016), [Complexity Classification of Local Hamiltonian Problems](https://doi.org/10.1137/140998287).
solved_when: An explicit, efficient witness-encryption construction is given for a natural hard StoqMA or stoquastic-Hamiltonian relation, together with a proof that its security relies on assumptions strictly weaker than those required for general QMA witness encryption.
why: It would identify a tractable quantum niche where witness encryption exists before solving the universal QMA-WE question, and would test whether stoquastic structure can be exploited cryptographically.
key_works: Cubitt–Montanaro (2016), [Complexity Classification of Local Hamiltonian Problems](https://doi.org/10.1137/140998287).

title: Succinct batch QMA-WE with finite witness budgets
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can many QMA conditions be encrypted into a single batch ciphertext of sublinear size, using only the finite number of supplied witness copies? More precisely, is there a witness encryption for conjunctions or thresholds of many QMA languages whose batch ciphertext size is sublinear in the number of conditions, subject to a finite witness-copy budget?
status: This is a proposed quantum extension of succinct batch NP witness encryption; the classical case is addressed by Devadas–Jain–Waters–Wu (2025/2026), [Succinct Witness Encryption for Batch Languages and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/944), and related classical verification of quantum states by Kalai–Khurana–Raizes (2026), [How to Classically Verify a Quantum Cat without Killing It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09282).
solved_when: A witness encryption scheme for conjunctions or thresholds of QMA conditions is constructed whose batch ciphertext size is sublinear in the batch size and whose decryption uses no more witness copies than supplied in the budget.
why: A solution would enable compact multi-condition quantum custody, allowing a single short ciphertext to enforce many QMA predicates at once without requiring unboundedly many copies of the quantum witnesses.
key_works: Devadas–Jain–Waters–Wu (2025/2026), [Succinct Witness Encryption for Batch Languages and Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/944); Kalai–Khurana–Raizes (2026), [How to Classically Verify a Quantum Cat without Killing It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09282).

title: Robust release thresholds for noisy quantum witnesses
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can a quantum witness be held and released under encryption on noisy hardware with provable guarantees? Specifically, derive concrete correctness and secrecy bounds relating physical witness noise, code overhead, the promise gap, and the false-release probability.
status: QMA robustness to constant witness noise is known, via Dziemba (2016), [Robustness of QMA against Witness Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.07332); encryption-specific resource budgets remain a proposed target.
solved_when: Explicit quantitative bounds are proved connecting physical witness noise, code overhead, promise gap, and false-release probability, for both correctness and secrecy.
why: It would make quantum witness custody meaningful on imperfect hardware rather than only in idealized noiseless settings.
key_works: Dziemba (2016), [Robustness of QMA against Witness Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.07332).

title: Cryptographic behavior near Hamiltonian promise gaps
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: What happens to cryptographic guarantees for Hamiltonian instances whose energies fall inside the promise gap, neither clearly above nor below the threshold? Either a graceful degradation of security and verification behavior should be specified for such intermediate instances, or it should be proved that discontinuities and unavoidable verification costs preclude any such specification.
status: This is a proposed frontier problem; standard QMA guarantees leave intermediate promise-gap instances unspecified. Related to the Quantum PCP conjecture and robust property testing; see Aharonov–Arad–Vidick (2013), [The Quantum PCP Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.7495).
solved_when: A complete characterization is given of the release behavior of cryptographic guarantees for instances near an energy threshold: either an explicit graceful-release specification covering intermediate promise-gap instances, or a proof that discontinuities and verification costs are unavoidable there.
why: Without such a characterization, ambiguous physical instances can be assigned security claims that no known guarantee supports.
key_works: Aharonov–Arad–Vidick (2013), [The Quantum PCP Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.7495).

title: Safe witness preservation against malicious ciphertexts
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can a verifier reject a malformed QMA-WE ciphertext without irreversibly destroying an honest single-copy witness? Formally, can noninteractive witness encryption achieve this guarantee under weaker setup assumptions than proving the complete encryptor computation?
status: Interactive witness-preserving verification is established in 2026; this noninteractive encryption guarantee is stronger. Key work: Kalai–Khurana–Raizes (2026), [How to Classically Verify a Quantum Cat without Killing It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09282).
solved_when: A noninteractive encryption scheme is constructed that rejects malformed QMA-WE ciphertexts while preserving an honest single-copy witness, under setup assumptions weaker than proving the complete encryptor computation.
why: Without it, simply submitting a ciphertext can serve as a witness-destruction attack, so ciphertext submission cannot be treated as a benign operation.
key_works: Kalai–Khurana–Raizes (2026), [How to Classically Verify a Quantum Cat without Killing It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09282).

title: Repeated decryption with imperfect quantum witnesses
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can a quantum credential survive being used to decrypt many times, and if so, how many uses can be bought with what loss in acceptance quality? More formally, what are the optimal tradeoffs among acceptance quality, cumulative measurement disturbance, and the number of decryptions, as conditions (such as the accepting subspaces) change?
status: High-completeness preservation is known, while low-quality witnesses and incompatible accepting subspaces pose different constraints; see Marriott–Watrous (2005), [Quantum Arthur–Merlin Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0506068), and Kalai–Khurana–Raizes (2026), [How to Classically Verify a Quantum Cat without Killing It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09282).
solved_when: A characterization of the optimal tradeoff curve between acceptance quality, cumulative disturbance, and decryption count is established, holding across changing conditions including low-quality witnesses and incompatible accepting subspaces.
why: It determines whether quantum credentials can support repeated use; without such a tradeoff, any scheme that consumes a quantum witness on first use cannot be safely recycled.
key_works: Marriott–Watrous (2005), [Quantum Arthur–Merlin Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0506068); Kalai–Khurana–Raizes (2026), [How to Classically Verify a Quantum Cat without Killing It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09282).

title: Hidden quantum verification conditions
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can the verification condition of a QMA verifier — the set of states it accepts — be hidden from all parties except through authorized leakage, under assumptions weaker than general quantum indistinguishability obfuscation, while remaining secure against adversaries that adaptively query witnesses?
status: This is a proposed privacy strengthening with no known construction. A natural starting point — null-circuit obfuscation, as studied by Bartusek–Malavolta (2022), [Indistinguishability Obfuscation of Null Quantum Circuits and Applications](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2022.15) — does not automatically hide non-null verification conditions, and general quantum obfuscation (Alagic–Fefferman (2016), [On Quantum Obfuscation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01771)) remains the only evident route, under assumptions the problem asks to weaken.
solved_when: A construction is given that obfuscates QMA verifier descriptions, leaks only the authorized information, satisfies adaptive witness-query security, and rests on assumptions strictly weaker than general quantum iO; alternatively, a proof that no such weaker-assumption construction exists.
why: It would enable private quantum eligibility tests and access-control policies where the accepting condition itself is a secret, something current quantum obfuscation tools do not provide.
key_works: Alagic–Fefferman (2016), [On Quantum Obfuscation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.01771); Bartusek–Malavolta (2022), [Indistinguishability Obfuscation of Null Quantum Circuits and Applications](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2022.15).

title: Compact witness pseudorandom-state generators
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Build compact public keys enabling NP-witness-gated preparation of keyed pseudorandom quantum states over exponential domains from post-quantum WE and pseudorandom states alone.
status: Proposed weaker-output primitive; classical WPRFs give a stronger-assumption baseline.
why: Could enable quantum credentials without full classical witness-PRF power.
key_works: Zhandry (2014/2016), [How to Avoid Obfuscation Using Witness PRFs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/301); Ji–Liu–Song (2018), [Pseudorandom Quantum States](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-96878-0_5).

title: Witness PRFs evaluated with quantum witnesses
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can we build witness PRFs that can be evaluated with quantum witnesses — a primitive that takes a QMA witness and produces a classical, witness-independent output, while giving the evaluator coherent public access to the computation and a clear rule for whether the witness is preserved or consumed?
status: This is a proposed quantum-native primitive. Existing classical WPRFs — Zhandry (2014/2016), [How to Avoid Obfuscation Using Witness PRFs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/301) — and QMA witness encryption — Bartusek–Malavolta (2022), [Indistinguishability Obfuscation of Null Quantum Circuits and Applications](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2022.15) — do not establish this combination.
solved_when: A construction of WPRFs for QMA relations is given with witness-independent classical outputs, coherent public evaluation, and explicit witness preservation or consumption rules, with security established.
why: Such a primitive would support reusable quantum-evidence-based key establishment, letting cryptographic keys be derived from quantum evidence without destroying the resource needed to derive them again.
key_works: Zhandry (2014/2016), [How to Avoid Obfuscation Using Witness PRFs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/301); Bartusek–Malavolta (2022), [Indistinguishability Obfuscation of Null Quantum Circuits and Applications](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2022.15).

title: Distributed quantum-witness decryption without reconstruction
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can a set of parties holding shares of a quantum witness jointly decrypt and act on it, with only minimal interaction among them, in a way that provably prevents any coalition from reconstructing the full witness or cloning a useful residual copy?
status: General interactive secure quantum computation, as in Ben-Or–Crépeau–Gottesman–Hassidim–Smith (2008), [Secure Multiparty Quantum Computation with (Only) a Strict Honest Majority](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.1544), supplies a baseline; the specialized low-interaction target remains open.
solved_when: A protocol is given that achieves distributed decryption of quantum-witness shares with minimal interaction and a proof that neither reconstruction of the whole witness nor useful residual cloning is possible.
why: It would enable threshold custody of quantum evidence, so that no single party or small coalition can unilaterally access or duplicate the underlying quantum witness.
key_works: Ben-Or–Crépeau–Gottesman–Hassidim–Smith (2008), [Secure Multiparty Quantum Computation with (Only) a Strict Honest Majority](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.1544).

title: Reproducible quantum-WE resource accounting
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can we produce reproducible, executable benchmarks that give a full resource accounting for quantum witness-encryption routes? Concretely, such benchmarks should report bits, qubits, witness copies, logical gates, non-Clifford costs, and ideal-oracle calls priced separately from the rest.
status: Currently only a proposed benchmark target; it is known that ideal-model feasibility does not supply concrete hardware costs. Key works: Bartusek–Jawale–Raizes–Tomer (2025/2026), [A New Approach to Arguments of Quantum Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05316); Kalai–Khurana–Raizes (2026), [How to Classically Verify a Quantum Cat without Killing It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09282).
solved_when: A published benchmark suite exists whose executable outputs report all of: classical bits, qubits, witness copies, logical gates, non-Clifford costs, and ideal-oracle calls accounted as a separately priced resource.
why: It makes competing quantum routes quantitatively comparable, replacing ideal-model feasibility arguments with concrete hardware costs.
key_works: Bartusek–Jawale–Raizes–Tomer (2025/2026), [A New Approach to Arguments of Quantum Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05316); Kalai–Khurana–Raizes (2026), [How to Classically Verify a Quantum Cat without Killing It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09282).

title: Erasure-free proactive sharing below extractable WE
subfield: Quantum language classes and witness resources
open: Can quantum proactive secret sharing be achieved without erasures, using only classical communication, from plain witness encryption and one-shot signatures rather than extractable witness encryption? More precisely: construct a scheme secure against mobile adversaries whose sole assumptions are post-quantum plain WE and one-shot signatures, eliminating the extractability requirement.
status: The 2026 baseline, due to Cojocaru–Kiayias–Shen–Wallden (2026), [Proactive Secret Sharing without Erasures](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1072), uses post-quantum classical extractable witness encryption. A subsequent LWE-based classical-upload certified-deletion compiler by Kalai–Raizes (2026), [Semi-Quantum Cryptography with Certified Deletion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38915), does not itself settle mobile-corruption proactive sharing.
solved_when: A construction of erasure-free quantum proactive secret sharing with classical communication is given, proven secure against mobile adversaries from post-quantum plain witness encryption and one-shot signatures, with no reliance on extractable witness encryption.
why: It reduces the assumptions needed for durable quantum-assisted custody, replacing extractable witness encryption with a weaker primitive.
key_works: Cojocaru–Kiayias–Shen–Wallden (2026), [Proactive Secret Sharing without Erasures](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1072); Kalai–Raizes (2026), [Semi-Quantum Cryptography with Certified Deletion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38915).

title: Matched-security WE benchmarking
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: How do current witness encryption constructions actually compare when run on the same relations and under the same security targets? A rigorous benchmark study is needed that reports, for identical workloads, the costs of setup, encryption, witness production, and decryption, together with memory and communication footprints.
status: A benchmark standard has been proposed, but published systems use materially different models and workloads. Key works include Uberti et al. (2021), [Building Usable Witness Encryption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04581); Fleischhacker–Hall-Andersen–Simkin (2024), [Extractable Witness Encryption for KZG Commitments and Efficient Laconic OT](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/264).
solved_when: A benchmark standard exists under which constructions are evaluated on identical relations and security targets, with reported measurements covering setup, encryption, witness production, decryption, memory, and communication.
why: It makes published claims of "faster" and "smaller" interpretable, allowing practitioners to choose constructions on evidence rather than incomparable workloads.
key_works: Uberti et al. (2021), [Building Usable Witness Encryption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04581); Fleischhacker–Hall-Andersen–Simkin (2024), [Extractable Witness Encryption for KZG Commitments and Efficient Laconic OT](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/264).

title: An adversarial relation dataset
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can we build a structured dataset of adversarial condition instances — ones that expose rank degeneracy, weak encodings, malformed constraints, and distribution-sensitive attacks — for benchmarking in this setting?
status: Currently a proposed data target, motivated by the 2026 ADP cryptanalysis of El Gebali et al. (2026), [Breaking ADP-Based Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1594).
solved_when: A publicly available dataset exists containing structured and adversarial condition instances covering rank degeneracy, weak encodings, malformed constraints, and distribution-sensitive attacks.
why: It prevents favorable random examples from defining the entire evaluation, forcing systems to be tested on inputs designed to break them.
key_works: El Gebali et al. (2026), [Breaking ADP-Based Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1594).

title: Independently audited general-NP implementation
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can we build a complete, end-to-end general-NP witness encryption implementation and validate it independently? The target is an implementation with a full security declaration, audited arithmetic, and independently reproduced cost figures.
status: The problem is currently a proposed deployment target. Existing implementations for special (non-general-NP) languages, and candidates that have been attacked, do not meet it. Key works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258); Hair–Sahai (2026), [Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275).
solved_when: A general-NP witness encryption implementation is delivered end-to-end, accompanied by a complete security declaration, whose arithmetic has been independently audited and whose costs have been independently reproduced.
why: It establishes a credible baseline against which all future efficiency improvements to witness encryption can be measured.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258); Hair–Sahai (2026), [Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275).

title: A versioned attack-and-repair ledger
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can we build a living, machine-readable ledger that ties each version of a cryptographic construction to its assumptions, the prerequisites of known attacks, reproduced failures, and the claims that still stand? The target is versioned infrastructure whose links update as constructions and attacks evolve.
status: Currently a proposed infrastructure target only; no such ledger exists, and the rapid 2025–2026 revisions of relevant constructions make static summaries unreliable. Key works motivating the need: Brzuska–Ünal–Woo (2024/2025), [Evasive LWE Assumptions: Definitions, Classes, and Counterexamples](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/2000); El Gebali et al. (2026), [Breaking ADP-Based Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1594).
solved_when: A maintained ledger exists that links construction versions, assumptions, attack prerequisites, reproduced failures, and surviving claims in machine-readable form, and remains reliable through the rapid 2025–2026 revision cycle.
why: It prevents obsolete security and performance claims from propagating, which static summaries cannot do when constructions are being revised this quickly.
key_works: Brzuska–Ünal–Woo (2024/2025), [Evasive LWE Assumptions: Definitions, Classes, and Counterexamples](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/2000); El Gebali et al. (2026), [Breaking ADP-Based Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1594).

title: A proof-preserving condition compiler
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can we build a compiler that turns typed condition specifications into supported witness-encryption (WE) relations, in a way that provably preserves the intended semantics and cleanly rejects features it cannot support?
status: This is currently a proposed systems target; practical special-language frameworks provide components that could be assembled toward it. Related work includes Polichlata (2026), [Practical Witness Encryption Schemes and Applications](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-243.html), alongside verified-compiler and secure-DSL design traditions.
solved_when: A compiler exists that translates typed condition specifications into supported WE relations, with a checked guarantee of semantic preservation and explicit rejection of unsupported features.
why: It makes condition design accessible to non-experts without silently weakening the intended policy — the failure mode would be a compiled relation that no longer enforces what the specification says.
key_works: Policharla (2026), [Practical Witness Encryption Schemes and Applications](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-243.html).

title: Full cost decomposition
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can the end-to-end cost of a cryptographic system be decomposed into separately measured stages — witness discovery, proof generation, verifier execution, encryption, and settlement — under realistic operating conditions?
status: Proposed as an experimental target; currently, headline encryption or on-chain cost figures often cover only one stage of the pipeline. Key work: Garg et al. (2026), [BABE: Verifying Proofs on Bitcoin Made 1000x Cheaper](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).
solved_when: A benchmark reports per-stage measurements for witness discovery, proof generation, verifier execution, encryption, and settlement across realistic conditions, rather than a single headline cost covering only one stage.
why: Without a full decomposition, a cryptographic speedup may look decisive while the true system bottleneck — which may lie in a different stage — remains unaddressed.
key_works: Garg et al. (2026), [BABE: Verifying Proofs on Bitcoin Made 1000x Cheaper](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).

title: Secure compression of matrix-based ciphertexts
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can structured matrix ciphertexts be compressed to remove their inherent redundancy without leaking new algebraic relations or invalidating the underlying security reduction? Formally: is there a compression scheme for such ciphertexts that provably preserves the original scheme's security, even against adversaries that exploit the algebraic structure the redundancy exposes?
status: This is a proposed target with no known construction; it has been observed that the redundancy present in such ciphertexts may itself enable attacks. Recent context comes from Soukhanov et al. (2026), [Implementable Witness Encryption from Arithmetic Affine Determinant Programs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/175), and El Gebali et al. (2026), [Breaking ADP-Based Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1594).
solved_when: A compression method for structured matrix ciphertexts is implemented and accompanied by an argument that the security reduction of the original scheme carries over unchanged, with no additional algebraic relations exposed by the compression.
why: Matrix-based schemes carry dominant storage and transport costs, so effective compression directly improves their practicality; conversely, the observed redundancy may itself be an attack surface, so unchecked compression could break security rather than save cost.
key_works: Soukhanov et al. (2026), [Implementable Witness Encryption from Arithmetic Affine Determinant Programs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/175); El Gebali et al. (2026), [Breaking ADP-Based Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1594).

title: Out-of-core and streaming WE
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can witness encryption be evaluated on ciphertexts far larger than a machine's RAM, so that evaluation streams through data with bounded working memory? Formally, the goal is an out-of-core evaluation procedure with predictable I/O patterns and no access pattern that leaks information about the witness.
status: Proposed as an engineering target; large candidate ciphertexts motivate the problem, but no secure baseline implementation has been established. Key work: Soukhanov et al. (2026), [Implementable Witness Encryption from Arithmetic Affine Determinant Programs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/175).
solved_when: An out-of-core/streaming evaluation implementation exists for witness-encryption ciphertexts exceeding RAM, achieving bounded working memory, predictable I/O, and no witness-dependent access leakage.
why: It makes large witness-encryption constructions evaluable on ordinary machines rather than requiring outsized memory.
key_works: Soukhanov et al. (2026), [Implementable Witness Encryption from Arithmetic Affine Determinant Programs](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/175).

title: Work, span, communication, and energy tradeoffs
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: What are the true parallel-complexity and communication costs of witness encryption, and can real implementations come close to those limits? Concretely, the question is to establish span and communication lower bounds for representative WE constructions and then engineer implementations that approach them.
status: The problem currently stands as a proposed quantitative program; it is recognized that wall-clock speed alone hides processor and communication costs. Key works: Hair–Sahai (2026), [Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275); Uberti et al. (2021), [Building Usable Witness Encryption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04581).
solved_when: For representative witness encryption constructions, provable work/span and communication lower bounds are established, and implementations are demonstrated whose processor usage, communication volume, and energy profile approach those bounds rather than merely optimizing wall-clock speed.
why: It guides realistic distributed acceleration: wall-clock speedups alone hide processor and communication costs, so without these tradeoffs understood, distributed deployments of witness encryption cannot be planned or costed credibly.
key_works: Hair–Sahai (2026), [Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275); Uberti et al. (2021), [Building Usable Witness Encryption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04581).

title: Accelerate the measured bottleneck on GPUs or FPGAs
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can the dominant operation of a reviewed witness-encryption workload be accelerated on GPUs or FPGAs so that end-to-end throughput measurably improves, with transfer, memory, and setup overheads all included in the measurement?
status: Currently a proposed moonshot-supporting engineering target; no qualifying end-to-end demonstration exists, and generic arithmetic speedups are explicitly noted as insufficient to establish end-to-end gains. Key work: Policharla (2026), [Practical Witness Encryption Schemes and Applications](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-243.html).
solved_when: A hardware implementation on GPU or FPGA is demonstrated for the dominant operation of a reviewed WE workload, and the reported gains account for transfer, memory, and setup overhead rather than isolated arithmetic speedups.
why: It converts practical special-language constructions into higher-throughput services; without end-to-end accounting, generic arithmetic speedups do not establish real gains.
key_works: Policharla (2026), [Practical Witness Encryption Schemes and Applications](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-243.html).

title: Amortization including setup debt
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: When does amortized cryptographic cost actually pay off? A measurement program is needed that accounts for total lifetime cost — setup, refresh, failed conditions, and unused preprocessing included — and establishes the break-even batch sizes at which a scheme becomes worthwhile.
status: Currently a proposed measurement target only. Key works motivating the problem: Policharla (2026), [Practical Witness Encryption Schemes and Applications](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-243.html); Garg et al. (2026), [BABE](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).
solved_when: Concrete break-even batch sizes and lifetime cost figures are established that incorporate setup, refresh, failed conditions, and unused preprocessing.
why: It determines which deployment volumes actually benefit, since low marginal cost can coexist with prohibitive total cost.
key_works: Policharla (2026), [Practical Witness Encryption Schemes and Applications](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-243.html); Garg et al. (2026), [BABE](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).

title: Constant-time witness handling
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can witness processing be implemented with explicit, end-to-end leakage guarantees — covering control-flow branches, memory access patterns, arithmetic operations, and early rejection paths — rather than relying on mathematical ciphertext security alone?
status: Currently a proposed implementation target; mathematical ciphertext security does not cover these channels. Verified arithmetic techniques such as Erbsen et al. (2019), [Simple High-Level Code For Cryptographic Arithmetic — With Proofs, Without Compromises](https://adam.chlipala.net/papers/FiatCryptoSP19/), are related prior art.
solved_when: An implementation exists whose witness handling is constant-time (or otherwise has stated leakage bounds) across branches, memory accesses, arithmetic, and early rejection, with the guarantees holding by construction or verification.
why: Valuable private proofs are exposed during decryption; without covering these channels, a mathematically secure ciphertext leaks its witness through physical side channels.
key_works: Erbsen et al. (2019), [Simple High-Level Code For Cryptographic Arithmetic — With Proofs, Without Compromises](https://adam.chlipala.net/papers/FiatCryptoSP19/).

title: Bounded hostile-input rejection
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can a public decryption endpoint be hardened so that oversized, malformed, or adversarially expensive ciphertexts and witnesses are rejected within explicit resource budgets, while all valid instances are still processed correctly?
status: This is currently a proposed service-hardening target around practical special-language deployments; no construction is recorded. Related areas include algorithmic complexity attacks and safe parsing.
solved_when: A rejection mechanism is constructed that meets the explicit resource budgets stated for the deployment, rejects all oversized, malformed, or adversarially expensive inputs within those budgets, and preserves correctness on valid instances.
why: It prevents public decryption endpoints from becoming denial-of-service amplifiers.
key_works: Adei–Madathil–Prasad–Reaves–Scafuro (2024), [Jäger: Automated Telephone Call Traceback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02839).

title: Interoperable negative test vectors
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can we publish a shared corpus of negative test vectors — covering invalid openings, wrong groups, malformed encodings, mixed statements, and boundary parameters — that works across independent implementations of these schemes?
status: A proposed infrastructure target; existing research code, such as the research-we-kzg implementation, is a starting point. Key works: Fleischhacker–Hall-Andersen–Simkin (2024), [Extractable Witness Encryption for KZG Commitments and Efficient Laconic OT](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/264); [research-we-kzg implementation](https://github.com/rot256/research-we-kzg).
solved_when: A cross-implementation set of negative test vectors exists, spanning invalid openings, wrong groups, malformed encodings, mixed statements, and boundary parameters, and is published for interoperable use.
why: Such vectors surface implementation disagreements before deployment, when they are cheap to fix rather than exploitable.
key_works: Fleischhacker–Hall-Andersen–Simkin (2024), [Extractable Witness Encryption for KZG Commitments and Efficient Laconic OT](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/264); [research-we-kzg implementation](https://github.com/rot256/research-we-kzg).

title: Verified condition-to-bytes pipelines
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
