open: Can the entire path from a condition's formal semantics down to the serialized ciphertext and witness bytes be verified end-to-end, including field encodings and domain separation?
status: This is currently a proposed integration target; verified arithmetic alone covers only part of the pipeline. Key works: Erbsen et al. (2019), [Simple High-Level Code For Cryptographic Arithmetic — With Proofs, Without Compromises](https://adam.chlipala.net/papers/FiatCryptoSP19/).
solved_when: A verified pipeline exists that connects a condition's formal semantics to its serialized bytes, covering field encodings and domain separation, so that verified arithmetic is no longer only a partial component of the pipeline.
why: Without it, representation mismatches at the encoding layer can bypass the very conditions the system is supposed to enforce.
key_works: Erbsen et al. (2019), [Simple High-Level Code For Cryptographic Arithmetic — With Proofs, Without Compromises](https://adam.chlipala.net/papers/FiatCryptoSP19/).

title: Bulk-data KEM binding
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can we build a key-encapsulation mechanism for condition encryption whose released key is cryptographically bound to the exact policy, payload, recipient restrictions, and epoch, so that substitution attacks cannot decouple the key from the condition it was issued for?
status: Currently a proposed integration target. The straightforward approach of simply encrypting a symmetric key leaves the binding and lifecycle questions open. Related lines of work include Fleischhacker–Hall-Andersen–Simkin (2024), [Extractable Witness Encryption for KZG Commitments and Efficient Laconic OT](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/264), and Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man's Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352); adjacent topics are committing KEMs and authenticated encryption.
solved_when: A condition-encryption KEM exists in which the released key is bound to the exact policy, payload, recipient restrictions, and epoch, and the construction resists substitution attacks on these bindings.
why: It makes large files and archives practical without encrypting them directly with witness encryption, and naive integration — simply encrypting a symmetric key — leaves the binding and lifecycle questions unresolved.
key_works: Fleischhacker–Hall-Andersen–Simkin (2024), [Extractable Witness Encryption for KZG Commitments and Efficient Laconic OT](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/264); Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).

title: Long-lived ciphertext migration
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can a pending ciphertext held in long-term storage be migrated to a new cryptographic assumption or implementation while provably preserving the access policy under which it was created, and while accounting for historical copies that survive the migration? The problem asks for a migration mechanism with checkable policy preservation and explicit treatment of retained older copies of the ciphertext.
status: Currently a proposed archival target; it is noted that publishing a stronger replacement cannot erase an older weak ciphertext, so historical copies must be dealt with directly. Key work: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man's Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).
solved_when: A migration procedure exists that moves pending ciphertexts across assumptions and implementations, carries a checkable guarantee that the policy is preserved, and explicitly handles retained historical copies of the ciphertext rather than assuming they are erased by a stronger replacement.
why: It supports conditions intended to remain pending for decades, where the original ciphertext may need to outlive the assumptions and implementations it was created under.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).

title: Witness-loss recovery
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can a system recover a user's access after the legitimate loss of a witness, using alternatives precommitted in advance, without those same mechanisms functioning as an unrestricted administrator bypass? Formally, recovery must be part of the security statement, since any recovery path changes the effective condition under which the asset is accessible.
status: Currently a proposed lifecycle target; no construction is known. It is recognized that recovery changes the effective condition and must be included in the security statement. Related directions include social recovery and threshold authentication, with connections to Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668) and Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man's Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).
solved_when: A recovery lifecycle exists in which precommitted alternative access paths restore lost legitimate access, and the security statement accounts for the changed effective condition, ruling out unrestricted administrator bypass.
why: Without it, conditional assets whose witnesses are lost become permanently inaccessible even though the underlying condition was valid; recovery prevents permanent loss of otherwise valid conditional assets.
key_works: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668); Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).

title: A verified 10× general-WE improvement
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can a general witness-encryption scheme be made ten times cheaper end-to-end — at matched security and workload — with the improvement actually demonstrated and verified rather than merely estimated? Formally, the goal is a reviewed general-WE construction exhibiting a named tenfold reduction in an end-to-end cost metric.
status: This is a proposed moonshot; no construction currently meets it. Gains observed in special-purpose languages, and estimates for candidate schemes obtained under attack, do not establish the record. Key works: Uberti et al. (2021), [Building Usable Witness Encryption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04581); Hair–Sahai (2026), [Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275).
solved_when: A reviewed general witness-encryption construction is shown, with verification, to achieve a 10× reduction in a named end-to-end cost, under matched security level and matched workload.
why: A solution would make witness encryption practical enough for occasional high-value applications such as proving theorems and archival uses that are out of reach at current costs.
key_works: Uberti et al. (2021), [Building Usable Witness Encryption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04581); Hair–Sahai (2026), [Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275).

title: A verified 1,000× general-WE improvement
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can we build a general witness-encryption scheme with a thousandfold matched-security improvement over current baselines, while reporting all preprocessing, proof, communication, and persistent-state costs? The target is a verified end-to-end efficiency gain, not a narrow or selectively measured one.
status: Proposed moonshot with no existing construction meeting it. BABE's narrower hybrid result (Garg et al. (2026), [BABE: Verifying Proofs on Bitcoin Made 1000x Cheaper](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf)) does not supply a universal general-WE baseline.
solved_when: A general witness-encryption construction demonstrates a 1,000× matched-security improvement, with full accounting of preprocessing, proof, communication, and persistent-state costs.
why: A solution could move conditional encryption from occasional escrow use toward recurring markets and agent work.
key_works: Garg et al. (2026), [BABE: Verifying Proofs on Bitcoin Made 1000x Cheaper](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).

title: Decryption near witness-verification cost
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can decryption be made to cost essentially the same as verifying the witness and reading the ciphertext, rather than substantially more? Formally, the goal is a construction whose decryption cost approaches witness-verification plus ciphertext-reading cost, under explicitly stated relation and security restrictions.
status: The problem is stated as a proposed asymptotic and concrete target; efficient constructions for special languages provide partial evidence toward it. Key works: Fleischhacker–Hall-Andersen–Simkin (2024), [Extractable Witness Encryption for KZG Commitments and Efficient Laconic OT](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/264); Hair–Sahai (2026), [Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275).
solved_when: A construction is given in which decryption cost asymptotically and concretely approaches the cost of checking the witness plus reading the ciphertext, for an explicitly specified class of relations and security restrictions.
why: It would make release overhead negligible once the evidence already exists — the decryptor pays almost nothing beyond what verifying the evidence itself costs.
key_works: Fleischhacker–Hall-Andersen–Simkin (2024), [Extractable Witness Encryption for KZG Commitments and Efficient Laconic OT](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/264); Hair–Sahai (2026), [Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18275).

title: Joules per conditional release
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: What does it actually cost, in joules, to run pervasive conditional-release cryptography as a deployed system? Concretely, measure the energy consumed per completed workload, accounting not only for proof generation but also for amortized setup, network transfer, and the wasted energy of failed releases.
status: The problem is at the stage of a proposed experimental baseline; currently, operation counts and transaction fees are used as stand-ins, and these are not energy measurements. Key works: Lloyd (2000), [Ultimate physical limits to computation](https://doi.org/10.1038/35023282); Garg et al. (2026), [BABE](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).
solved_when: A reproducible experimental baseline exists reporting energy per completed workload that includes proof generation, setup amortization, network transfer, and failed releases — as opposed to proxies such as operation counts or transaction fees.
why: It determines whether encrypting data for conditional release everywhere is energetically credible, or whether the energy cost rules out large-scale deployment.
key_works: Lloyd (2000), [Ultimate physical limits to computation](https://doi.org/10.1038/35023282); Garg et al. (2026), [BABE](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).

title: Physical-resource lower-bound decomposition
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: Can the cost of witness encryption be decomposed so that the portion forced by physics — verification work, communication, storage, and physical timing — is cleanly separated from the overhead that comes only from the particular cryptographic construction? More formally, is there a framework that derives lower bounds on these physical-resource costs independently of any specific scheme?
status: Currently a proposed lower-bound program; known physical computation bounds do not directly yield tight WE bounds. Related to Lloyd (2000), [Ultimate physical limits to computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9908043); connected themes include Landauer bounds, communication latency, and reversible computing.
solved_when: A decomposition is given that isolates the unavoidable physical-resource costs (verification, communication, storage, and timing) from construction-specific cryptographic overhead, with tight bounds on the physical component.
why: It gives the physics-limit scenario a precise meaning, turning a vague "how cheap can this possibly be?" question into separable, analyzable quantities.
key_works: Lloyd (2000), [Ultimate physical limits to computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9908043).

title: Encryption cost versus witness-discovery cost
subfield: Engineering, benchmarks, and efficiency frontiers
open: For which application regimes does encryption, witness discovery, or verification dominate the total cost? A mapping built on measured workloads and explicit search distributions would identify where each phase is the bottleneck.
status: Proposed as a data target; no mapping yet exists. It is noted that efficient encryption cannot make difficult theorem proving or optimization easy. Key works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258); Lloyd (2000), [Ultimate physical limits to computation](https://doi.org/10.1038/35023282).
solved_when: A data-driven map of application regimes exists, based on measured workloads and explicit search distributions, showing which of encryption, witness discovery, or verification dominates in each regime.
why: It directs research toward improvements that change actual feasibility, since efficient encryption alone cannot make difficult theorem proving or optimization easy.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258); Lloyd (2000), [Ultimate physical limits to computation](https://doi.org/10.1038/35023282).

title: Sustained independent cryptanalysis funding
subfield: Funding, maintenance, and governance
open: Can a standing funding program be established that supports independent cryptanalysis — reproducible attacks, negative results, parameter audits, and maintained challenge instances — financially independent of the proponents of the constructions under scrutiny?
status: Currently a proposed funding gap: public ADP challenge material exists, but no monetary award for this exact program has been verified. Key works: [[alloc]init] (2026), [Cryptographic Challenges for AADP WE](https://www.allocinit.xyz/posts/challenges); El Gebali et al. (2026), [Breaking ADP-Based Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1594).
solved_when: A sustained monetary award program exists, verified as active, dedicated to this exact scope of independent cryptanalysis work.
why: It turns security confidence from episodic, proponent-funded claims into a maintained public good, ensuring constructions face continuous adversarial scrutiny.
key_works: [[alloc]init] (2026), [Cryptographic Challenges for AADP WE](https://www.allocinit.xyz/posts/challenges); El Gebali et al. (2026), [Breaking ADP-Based Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1594).

title: Maintained reference-stack funding
subfield: Funding, maintenance, and governance
open: Can the cryptographic community secure durable funding to maintain interoperable implementations, test corpora, documentation, and independent review as shared infrastructure rather than byproducts of individual research grants?
status: Currently only a proposed funding target; research prototypes demonstrate feasibility of the underlying infrastructure but do not provide long-term maintenance. Key works: [research-we-kzg](https://github.com/rot256/research-we-kzg); Adei et al. (2024), [Jäger: Automated Telephone Call Traceback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02839).
solved_when: A sustained funding mechanism exists that supports reference implementations, test corpora, documentation, and independent review over the long term, beyond the lifetime of any single research grant.
why: Without it, every application must rebuild fragile cryptographic infrastructure on its own, multiplying cost and risk.
key_works: [research-we-kzg](https://github.com/rot256/research-we-kzg); Adei et al. (2024), [Jäger: Automated Telephone Call Traceback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02839).

title: Standardized security declarations
subfield: Funding, maintenance, and governance
open: Can the cryptographic community agree on a standardized, interoperable vocabulary for declaring the security guarantees of witness encryption schemes? In particular, such declarations should distinguish false-instance versus hard-true security, setup assumptions, extractability, adaptivity, quantum access, and revocation semantics.
status: This is a proposed infrastructure target; no such standard exists today, and the word "WE" currently covers materially different guarantees. Key works: Bellare–Hoang (2013/2015), [Adaptive Witness Encryption and Asymmetric Password-based Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/704); Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).
solved_when: A set of interoperable security declarations exists that covers false-instance versus hard-true security, setup, extractability, adaptivity, quantum access, and revocation semantics, replacing the single blanket term "WE" that currently spans materially different guarantees.
why: Standardized declarations would make procurement decisions, composition arguments, and benchmark comparisons assessable rather than ambiguous across schemes with divergent guarantees.
key_works: Bellare–Hoang (2013/2015), [Adaptive Witness Encryption and Asymmetric Password-based Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/704); Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).

title: Correction and appeal before irreversible release
subfield: Funding, maintenance, and governance
open: How can a system offer a funded, precommitted window for correcting or appealing an erroneous event certificate — with adjudication rules fixed in advance — without giving anyone unrestricted power to cancel events after the fact? Formally, the challenge is to design correction and appeal mechanisms that preserve the irreversibility guarantees of the release mechanism while admitting bounded, accountable revision.
status: This is currently a proposed governance target only; no such design is realized, and disclosed plaintext cannot be recalled by a later appeal. Related lines of work include Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352), and Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).
solved_when: A concrete design exists for funded, precommitted correction windows and adjudication rules that corrects erroneous event certificates without granting unrestricted cancellation authority.
why: It makes irreversible automation usable in settings where the underlying evidence can be disputed; without it, disclosed plaintext cannot be recalled by a later appeal, so any error is permanent.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352); Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).

title: Hard-true theorem bounty confidentiality
subfield: Theorem bounties and formal mathematical economies
open: Can a bounty for a formal proof be posted offline, in a way that remains confidential when the underlying theorem is actually true? Formally, is it possible to secure an offline bounty for polynomially bounded formal proofs under the theorem's actual distribution and any auxiliary information, in the hard-true case?
status: Proposed as an application target. Ordinary witness encryption only guarantees privacy for false instances; hard-true protection needs additional justification. Key work: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258).
solved_when: A scheme is exhibited that secures an offline bounty for polynomially bounded formal proofs, maintaining privacy even when the theorem is true, under its actual theorem distribution and auxiliary information.
why: It establishes the central confidentiality premise behind theorem bounties; without hard-true protection, the bounty leaks information precisely in the case that matters most.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258).

title: Claimant-bound noninteractive proof rewards
subfield: Theorem bounties and formal mathematical economies
open: Can a previously unknown solver of a mathematical problem redeem a bounty for a noninteractive proof without ever revealing a secret that would let others copy the redemption, and without allowing the payout to be redirected to a different claimant? Formally, one seeks a mechanism binding redemption rights to the proof's creator, so relayers and observers cannot substitute themselves as the recipient.
status: The problem is proposed as a 1,000×-tier extension of prior work; noninteractive computational bounties were formalized in 2014 by Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).
solved_when: A construction is given in which offline-created, noninteractive proof bounties can be redeemed by their unknown solvers with no copyable redemption secret exposed and no payout-identity substitution possible — the 1,000×-tier extension of the 2014 noninteractive computational bounty formalization.
why: Without it, anyone who relays or observes a valid proof can steal the reward, so solvers cannot safely publish proofs before being paid.
key_works: Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).

title: Publicly verifiable bounty backing
subfield: Theorem bounties and formal mathematical economies
open: How can a bounty sponsor prove, to anyone checking on-chain, that an encrypted commitment really backs the advertised reward with unspent funds, commits to the exact bounty predicate, and cannot be revoked or invalidated by a key the sponsor quietly kept?
status: A proposed integration target only; as things stand, encrypted wallet keys alone permit sponsor theft. Related to proof of reserves, fair exchange (Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740)), and escrow solvency.
solved_when: A publicly verifiable construction exists in which the advertised ciphertext provably controls the promised unspent reward, is bound to the exact predicate, and remains valid even against a sponsor holding retained keys.
why: It turns an encrypted promise into verifiable funded escrow; without it, sponsors can post ciphertexts that look funded but are actually theft-prone shells.
key_works: Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740).

title: Assumption-audited formal bounty checkers
subfield: Theorem bounties and formal mathematical economies
open: Can we build a bounty checker that cryptographically binds a sponsor's mathematical statement to exactly the verification procedure that decides payment? Concretely, the proposition, permitted axioms, kernel version, imports, and elaboration semantics must all be tied to the exact encrypted verifier so no gap remains between sponsor intent and the compiled acceptance relation.
status: Proposed integration target; formal kernels exist, but sponsor intent must be connected to the compiled acceptance relation. Key works: de Moura–Ullrich (2021), [The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37).
solved_when: A working integration exists in which the encrypted verifier verifiably enforces the bound between the stated proposition and its permitted axioms, kernel version, imports, and elaboration semantics, such that no unintended axioms or altered statements can authorize payment.
why: Without this binding, a solver could exploit unintended axioms or an altered statement to trigger payout, breaking the integrity of formal bounty economies.
key_works: de Moura–Ullrich (2021), [The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37).

title: Proof-length renewal without changing the theorem
subfield: Theorem bounties and formal mathematical economies
open: Can a bounty's required proof-size or verification-time bounds be renewed after the fact — replaced with new bounds for the same unaltered theorem and the same committed funding — in a way that explicitly handles sponsor participation and the generation of replacement ciphertexts?
status: Proposed target only; it is noted that arbitrary huge binary-encoded bounds do not automatically define NP relations. Key works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258).
solved_when: A renewal procedure exists that preserves the proposition and its funding while updating proof-size or verification-time bounds, with explicit requirements for sponsor participation and replacement ciphertexts fully specified.
why: It keeps long-lived prizes usable as formal proof technology changes, so a bounty does not become obsolete when proof systems evolve.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258).

title: Symmetric proof-or-refutation escrow
subfield: Theorem bounties and formal mathematical economies
open: Can we design an escrow mechanism that pays out bounties symmetrically — funding either an allowed formal proof or a checkable counterexample of a precisely formalized claim — while correctly isolating the rewards for each branch and remaining sound when branches are nonexhaustive or the axiom system is inconsistent?
status: Proposed target only. Composing witness-encryption branches in the style of Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258), supplies no decision procedure for arbitrary mathematics.
solved_when: A construction exists that handles both payout branches (proof and refutation) with branch rewards isolated, and remains well-defined for nonexhaustive branches and inconsistent axioms.
why: It supplies balanced incentives for resolving a formally specified mathematical claim, enabling bounty economies where neither provers nor disprovers are structurally favored.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters (2013), [Witness Encryption and its Applications](https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/258).

title: Lemma-DAG rewards resistant to contribution splitting
subfield: Theorem bounties and formal mathematical economies
open: Can a formal proof economy reward contributors along a lemma dependency graph so that splitting one contribution into several lemmas — or restating the same lemma in syntactically different but equivalent forms — cannot inflate payouts, even when participants collude? Formally, this asks for a budget-preserving reward mechanism over theorem-proving dependency DAGs that is invariant to syntactic decomposition and equivalent restatement.
status: A 1,000×-tier mechanism has been proposed; its known limitation is that validity alone does not measure contribution. Related work includes Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).
solved_when: A mechanism is specified and proven to preserve the payout budget under arbitrary contribution splitting, equivalent restatements, and collusion among contributors.
why: It would enable cumulative proof economies, where many contributors are rewarded for building on each other's lemmas, instead of winner-take-all prizes that compensate only the first complete proof.
key_works: Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).

title: Long-lived proof-checker migration
subfield: Theorem bounties and formal mathematical economies
open: Can an escrowed theorem be carried intact across generations of proof kernels and encodings, so that it remains verifiable decades after the system it was written for is retired? Formally, this asks for a migration procedure that produces checkable semantic-equivalence certificates between the old and new checker settings while correctly accounting for historical ciphertexts retained under the old scheme.
status: Currently a proposed 10×-tier archival target; it is recognized that version pinning alone does not solve semantic migration. Related directions include proof translation, verified compiler bootstrapping, and archival security. Key work: de Moura–Ullrich (2021), [The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37).
solved_when: A migration mechanism exists that moves theorem escrows across kernels and encodings via semantic-equivalence certificates that are independently checkable, and that handles retained historical ciphertexts — meeting the proposed 10×-tier archival target.
why: Without it, version pinning leaves escrowed theorems stranded as their proof systems evolve, so prizes cannot survive decades of proof-system evolution.
key_works: de Moura–Ullrich (2021), [The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37).

title: Censorship-aware missed-heartbeat certificates
subfield: Dead-man switches, inheritance, and durable custody
open: Can a dead-man switch release its secret based on a cryptographic certificate that finalized heartbeats were *not* included — rather than merely absent — with a quantified false-release risk under censorship, network partitions, and delayed message delivery?
status: Proposed as an extension beyond 2026 UC dead-man-switch constructions of Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352); no such censorship-aware non-inclusion certificate currently exists.
solved_when: A construction exists that triggers release only on finalized heartbeat non-inclusion and proves a quantitative bound on false-release probability under censorship, partitions, and delayed delivery.
why: It prevents network failures from being silently interpreted as the intended real-world event, since log absence alone does not certify physical death.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).

title: Private heartbeats with public recovery
subfield: Dead-man switches, inheritance, and durable custody
open: Can a dead-man switch keep every sensitive fact private — that it exists, who its nominees are, and when heartbeats are due — while still allowing verifiable recovery by the right parties and provably bounding false releases? The question includes hiding traffic metadata, not just the switch statement itself.
status: This is a proposed extension beyond statement hiding and the 2026 DMS baseline, building toward techniques suggested by Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668); no construction currently achieves the full goal.
solved_when: A construction is given that hides switch installation, nominees, and heartbeat schedules (including traffic metadata), while achieving verifiable recovery and a bounded false-release rate; a matching formal definition and security analysis for this stronger setting completes the theory.
why: Without it, the mere existence of a switch leaks sensitive relationships; solving it enables durable-custody and inheritance protocols that do not expose who stands to inherit or who is being monitored.
key_works: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).

title: Optimal revocation with copied ciphertexts
subfield: Dead-man switches, inheritance, and durable custody
open: What is the least amount of online state, freshness checking, or trusted erasure needed to make revocation of copied pending ciphertexts actually work, and what tradeoff curve between these resources and achievable revocation guarantees is attainable?
status: It is known that static ciphertexts combined with valid witnesses defeat unconditional revocation; the open target concerns the guarantees achievable when extra resources are allowed. Key works: Goyal et al. (2022), [Storing and Retrieving Secrets on a Blockchain](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~bparno/papers/eweb.pdf).
solved_when: A characterization is given of the minimum online state, freshness checks, or trusted erasure required for revocation of copied pending ciphertexts, together with a construction attaining the resulting tradeoff.
why: It clarifies which cancellation promises in durable-custody and dead-man-switch systems can actually be implemented, separating unconditional revocation from what extra resources buy.
key_works: Goyal et al. (2022), [Storing and Retrieving Secrets on a Blockchain](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~bparno/papers/eweb.pdf).

title: Beneficiary-only release despite key loss
subfield: Dead-man switches, inheritance, and durable custody
open: Can a custody scheme combine event evidence (such as proof of death), nominee authentication, and preauthorized lost-key recovery so that a beneficiary can be released their inheritance, without the combination ever yielding an administrator's universal bypass? More precisely, design a lifecycle in which each recovery path is independently sound yet no party or coalition gains the power to unlock funds outside the authorized beneficiary-only conditions.
status: Currently a proposed lifecycle extension; authorized multi-recipient recovery already appears in Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man's Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).
solved_when: A scheme is specified and implemented that (i) grants release only to designated beneficiaries upon verified event evidence, (ii) authenticates nominees, (iii) supports preauthorized recovery of lost keys by multiple recipients, and (iv) provably or demonstrably prevents any administrator-level universal bypass across these mechanisms.
why: Without it, long-term inheritance and institutional custody are either unrecoverable when keys are lost or recoverable only by granting a trusted party dangerous universal unlock power.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).

title: Continuity under correlated committee churn
subfield: Dead-man switches, inheritance, and durable custody
open: Can a secret and its release policy be kept continuously available through correlated committee churn — simultaneous departures, loss of quorum, and subsequent recovery — without the system accumulating historical shares as committees change?
status: This is a proposed extension of evolving-committee sharing to the setting where the dealer becomes permanently unavailable. Key works: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352); Campanelli et al. (2022), [Encryption to the Future](https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/1423).
solved_when: A scheme is given in which secrets and release policies survive correlated departures, quorum loss, and recovery, with no accumulation of historical shares across committee evolutions (and correct operation even after the dealer becomes permanently unavailable).
why: It supports archives that outlive their original operators, enabling durable custody and inheritance-style dead-man switches even when committees fail in a correlated way.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352); Campanelli et al. (2022), [Encryption to the Future](https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/1423).

title: Composable release-or-delete policies
subfield: Dead-man switches, inheritance, and durable custody
open: Can release-or-delete policies for encrypted records be composed so that deleting access to a record also protects it against adversaries who kept old ciphertexts? In particular, what erasure or mutable-mediation assumptions are necessary for such composition to be sound?
status: Release and delete modes are constructed in 2026; copied classical witness-encryption ciphertexts are not thereby deletable. Key work: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).
solved_when: A construction (or impossibility) of composable record-specific release and deletion rules is given, together with an identification of the erasure or mutable-mediation assumptions required to resist adversaries retaining old ciphertexts.
why: It would support differentiated retention policies without relying on impossible promises to cancel already-released data.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).

title: Policy-preserving disaster recovery
subfield: Dead-man switches, inheritance, and durable custody
open: Can a dead-man switch or long-term custody scheme recover from failures of its own infrastructure — dead clocks, lost logs, or collapsed release services — while still enforcing exactly the release policy its owner intended? In other words, can recovery follow precommitted rules that resist manufactured failures and preserve the intended predicate rather than opening the door to whoever triggers the "disaster"?
status: Only a proposed 10×-tier archival target exists; component redundancy does not establish safe migration. Related work includes Gailly et al. (2023), [tlock: Practical Timelock Encryption from Threshold BLS](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/189).
solved_when: An engineering design and implementation achieves the proposed 10×-tier archival target, providing recovery of failed clocks, logs, or release services through precommitted rules such that component redundancy alone is not the basis of safety — safe migration is explicitly established.
why: Without such a mechanism, a single obsolete service can permanently strand ciphertexts, locking owners and heirs out of data that can never be released.
key_works: Gailly et al. (2023), [tlock: Practical Timelock Encryption from Threshold BLS](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/189).

title: Compile event meaning into certificate predicates
subfield: Encryption to future events and authenticated reality
open: When a ciphertext or contract is tied to a real-world event, how do we guarantee the certificate that unlocks it actually captures what the event means — the right sources, units, timestamps, revisions, and interpretation — rather than merely what some oracle attests? Formally, can we compile event specifications into acceptance predicates in a way that certifiably binds all of these dimensions during the translation?
status: Proposed integration target; authenticated source claims do not establish physical truth. Key works: Zhang et al. (2020), [DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.00938). Related: data provenance; semantic interoperability; verified parsing.
solved_when: A compiler exists that takes an event specification and produces an acceptance relation whose certificates verifiably encode source identity, units, timestamps, revision state, and interpretation semantics, so that a technically valid certificate cannot authorize an unintended condition.
why: Without such binding, an attacker can obtain a perfectly valid certificate over the wrong data, revision, or interpretation and unlock a condition that was never intended to trigger — the cryptography checks out while the meaning is wrong.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2020), [DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.00938).

title: Multi-source disagreement rules
subfield: Encryption to future events and authenticated reality
open: How should a system aggregate multiple conflicting authenticated reports of the same real-world event into a trustworthy verdict, when some sources may be faulty or their evidence correlated, and when adversaries can strategically choose which sources to consult? The goal is a disagreement rule that operates under explicit fault and correlation assumptions and resists such strategic source selection.
status: Currently only a proposed target; the nearest existing primitive, threshold signatures, counts key holders rather than independent observations. Key works: Zhang et al. (2016), [Town Crier: An Authenticated Data Feed for Smart Contracts](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/168); Madathil et al. (2023), [Cryptographic Oracle-Based Conditional Payments](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/499).
solved_when: A construction and analysis exist that aggregate conflicting authenticated reports under stated fault and correlation assumptions and provably prevent strategic source selection.
why: It would make irreversible releases (e.g., funds unlocked by future events) robust to correlated or disputed evidence, closing a gap between key-holder consensus and independent observation.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2016), [Town Crier: An Authenticated Data Feed for Smart Contracts](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/168); Madathil et al. (2023), [Cryptographic Oracle-Based Conditional Payments](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/499).

title: Equivocation-resistant event finalization
subfield: Encryption to future events and authenticated reality
open: Can we design a release mechanism that refuses to act on provisional or equivocating certificates, releasing information only once the underlying event is genuinely settled according to explicit challenge periods and correction rules?
status: Currently a proposed target; no construction is known. Later corrections cannot retract disclosed information. Related to transparency logs, finality, and optimistic adjudication; see Zhang et al. (2016), [Town Crier: An Authenticated Data Feed for Smart Contracts](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/168).
solved_when: A mechanism is specified in which disclosure occurs only for events that have passed a defined challenge period under stated correction rules, and equivocating or provisional certificates provably cannot trigger release.
why: It aligns irreversible release with evidence finality: once information is disclosed, later corrections cannot retract it, so releasing on unsettled evidence is permanently damaging.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2016), [Town Crier: An Authenticated Data Feed for Smart Contracts](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/168).

title: Future-attestation key migration
subfield: Encryption to future events and authenticated reality
open: Can a system that encrypts conditions to an institution's attesting key keep those conditions valid and provably protected when the key is later compromised and replaced? The goal is a construction in which migration to a new key follows historically authenticated rules, and ciphertexts encrypted under the old key retain explicit, stated guarantees.
status: This is currently a proposed archival target only; no construction is known, and it is observed that replacing a key does not automatically repair previously encrypted conditions. Related lines include forward-secure signatures and archival timestamping, with foundational work by Haber–Stornetta (1991), [How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-38424-3_32).
solved_when: A construction exists that carries conditions across attesting-key compromise and replacement via historically authenticated migration rules, with explicit guarantees for old ciphertexts stated and proven.
why: Without it, long-horizon event encryption breaks the moment an institution rotates or loses a key, since replacing the key does not automatically repair previously encrypted conditions.
key_works: Haber–Stornetta (1991), [How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-38424-3_32).

title: Geographic fairness after witness publication
subfield: Encryption to future events and authenticated reality
open: How should optimal access fairness be defined when participants have asymmetric connectivity and face selective dissemination, and can explicit information-advantage bounds be approached under such a definition? A formal treatment would quantify the informational edge held by better-connected or better-placed recipients after a common release event.
status: A physics-limit target has been proposed: common release events cannot remove propagation delay. Key works: Liu et al. (2015/2018), [How to build time-lock encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/482).
solved_when: A definition of optimal access fairness under asymmetric connectivity and selective dissemination is given, together with explicit information-advantage bounds that are approached (matched) by a construction.
why: It matters for auctions, markets, and geographically distributed recipients, where propagation-based advantage translates directly into unequal access to released information.
key_works: Liu et al. (2015/2018), [How to build time-lock encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/482).

title: Bounded nonoccurrence certificates
subfield: Encryption to future events and authenticated reality
open: Can we cryptographically certify that no qualifying event occurred within a bounded time interval, building on authenticated nonmembership proofs together with an explicit completeness assumption?
status: Proposed target; no construction is known. The core obstacles identified are that log absence differs from unobserved physical nonoccurrence, and arbitrary negative conditions need not be NP-verifiable. Related to Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man's Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).
solved_when: A construction exists that certifies nonoccurrence of a qualifying event over a bounded interval via authenticated nonmembership, under an explicit completeness assumption distinguishing logged absence from unobserved physical nonoccurrence.
why: It would enable carefully specified timeout and fallback conditions, such as dead man's switch style protocols that trigger only when an event provably did not occur.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2026), [Dead Man’s Switch Cryptography](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1352).

title: Condition privacy against candidate-event testing
subfield: Encryption to future events and authenticated reality
open: Can a witness-encryption-style scheme hide the very policy or condition under which a ciphertext can be opened, even against an adversary who enumerates candidate events in public and correlates ciphertexts? The goal is condition privacy against candidate-event testing, with the leakage of successful and failed tests made explicit.
status: This is a proposed extension beyond statement hiding. A caveat is that cheaper decryption can amplify dictionary attacks. Related concerns are search-pattern privacy and predicate dictionary attacks. Key work: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).
solved_when: A scheme is constructed that hides policies against public candidate-witness enumeration and cross-ciphertext correlation, together with a formal accounting of leakage from successful and failed tests.
why: It protects private interests and contingent plans, ensuring that encrypting to a future event does not itself reveal which event or plan is at stake.
key_works: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).

title: Persistent future-witness availability
subfield: Encryption to future events and authenticated reality
open: How can we preserve reconstructible event certificates — together with their source chains, validity periods, and verifier bindings — after the original source disappears? Formally, the goal is an archival construction that retains the qualifying evidence needed for future-witness decryption even once the sources attesting those witnesses are gone.
status: Currently only a proposed archival target; retaining ciphertexts does not retain qualifying evidence. Related to Goyal et al. (2022), [Storing and Retrieving Secrets on a Blockchain](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~bparno/papers/eweb.pdf), with connections to digital preservation, data availability, and evidentiary provenance.
solved_when: A construction exists that keeps event certificates reconstructible with their full source chains, validity periods, and verifier bindings after the original source disappears, so that a satisfied condition remains decryptable rather than merely retaining ciphertexts.
why: Without it, satisfied conditions can become permanently undecryptable, since retaining ciphertexts does not retain the qualifying evidence needed to decrypt them.
key_works: Goyal et al. (2022), [Storing and Retrieving Secrets on a Blockchain](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~bparno/papers/eweb.pdf).

title: Disclosure atomicity across probabilistic finality
subfield: Conditional markets, cross-ledger escrow, and auctions
open: Can an irreversible disclosure of information be bound atomically to a payment when buyer and seller use different ledgers whose finality is only probabilistic? Formally: construct a cross-ledger exchange in which the amount of information disclosed without corresponding payment is bounded even when ledgers reorganize or parties withhold messages.
status: The problem is posed as a strengthening of fair exchange: currently, plaintext cannot roll back together with a payment. Key work: Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740). Related directions include atomic swaps, probabilistic consensus, and fair exchange.
solved_when: A construction (with proof) is given in which the disclosure leaked absent a completed payment is bounded by an explicit quantity, robust to ledger reorganizations and message withholding across ledgers with different finality guarantees.
why: It would make sales of information across distinct systems credible — a seller cannot lose the plaintext to a payment that later rolls back.
key_works: Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740).

title: Deposit-isolated WE bridge authority
subfield: Conditional markets, cross-ledger escrow, and auctions
open: Can a bridge authority authorize exactly one designated withdrawal from a remote-state witness without ever exposing reusable custody keys, while proving value conservation under replay? Formally, the goal is a construction in which single-use spending authority is bound to the witnessed remote state, so that replayed authorizations are provably value-conserving.
status: This is a proposed deployment target; BABE combines linear-pairing witness encryption with interaction. Key works: Garg et al. (2026), [BABE: Verifying Proofs on Bitcoin Made 1000x Cheaper](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).
solved_when: A construction exists that (i) authorizes exactly one designated withdrawal per witness, (ii) keeps custody keys non-reusable and unexposed, and (iii) carries a proof of value conservation under replay.
why: It would let proof-conditioned bridges expose only the intended spending authority, so a compromised or replayed authorization cannot drain custody repeatedly.
key_works: Garg et al. (2026), [BABE: Verifying Proofs on Bitcoin Made 1000x Cheaper](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).

title: Permissionless claimant entry after setup
subfield: Conditional markets, cross-ledger escrow, and auctions
open: Can new proof producers join an already-deployed escrow without performing pairwise setup with the original participants, while fairness and bounded disputes are preserved? A construction achieving this would yield permissionless claimant entry after setup.
status: Proposed extension only; existing setup-interactive constructions do not automatically yield permanently offline universal public escrow. Key work: Garg et al. (2026), [BABE: Verifying Proofs on Bitcoin Made 1000x Cheaper](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).
solved_when: A construction exists in which new claimants enter existing escrows without pairwise setup with original participants, and the scheme retains fairness and bounded disputes.
why: It opens conditional markets to participants who arrive after deployment, rather than locking out anyone not present at setup.
key_works: Garg et al. (2026), [BABE: Verifying Proofs on Bitcoin Made 1000x Cheaper](https://docs.babylonlabs.io/papers/BABE_Research_Paper_Jan_2026.pdf).

title: Sealed auctions with proof-bound clearing
subfield: Conditional markets, cross-ledger escrow, and auctions
open: Can a sealed auction be run so that bids remain sealed until the submission set is definitively fixed, with the winner, price, and settlement publicly proven consistent? Formally, this asks for a construction combining bid sealing with proof-bound clearing over the committed set.
status: A 1,000×-tier integration has been proposed, but batched threshold encryption supplies only part of the contract; no full construction is known. Key work: Policharla (2026), [Practical Witness Encryption Schemes and Applications](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-243.html).
solved_when: A working construction exists that unlocks bids only after the submission set is fixed and produces proofs of consistent winner, price, and settlement rules.
why: It prevents premature bid opening and selective-clearing manipulation, which currently break trust in sealed-auction settings.
key_works: Policharla (2026), [Practical Witness Encryption Schemes and Applications](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-243.html).

title: Private-data conditional market settlement
subfield: Conditional markets, cross-ledger escrow, and auctions
open: Can mutually distrusting parties settle a contract whose payout depends on private, authenticated real-world observations — without revealing the underlying records, and without anyone being able to cherry-pick which observations get reported? Formally: settle precommitted payout functions on authenticated private data while proving completeness of the observation window and resisting selective reporting.
status: Proposed as an extension of private-data instruments; correlated contracts are noted to create additional leakage. Related key work: Zhang et al. (2020), [DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.00938).
solved_when: A settlement mechanism exists that (i) evaluates precommitted payout functions on authenticated private observations, (ii) proves that all observations in the committed window were considered, and (iii) prevents selective reporting; correlated contracts must not introduce additional leakage beyond the single-contract case.
why: It would enable contingent exchange — conditional payments, escrow, and auction outcomes — without publishing the underlying records on which the conditions depend.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2020), [DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.00938).

title: Multiasset, multi-condition atomic release
subfield: Conditional markets, cross-ledger escrow, and auctions
open: Can several parties, each holding a different asset on a different ledger, settle an arbitrary Boolean combination of conditions so that either all releases happen or none does — with abort compensation paid explicitly to the parties harmed by a failed settlement — using the weakest possible coordination resource? In other words, characterize the minimal shared primitive that suffices to atomically consume a multi-condition predicate across multiple assets.
status: The problem is currently a proposed generalization; it is known that ciphertext composition does not implement atomic consumption. Key work: Gomez-Martinez et al. (2024/2025), [Algebraic Zero Knowledge Contingent Payment](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1930).
solved_when: A construction (with proof) realizes all-or-nothing release for Boolean combinations of multiple parties' proofs, includes explicit abort compensation, and is matched by a lower bound showing the coordination resource used is the weakest possible; no weaker resource can achieve the same atomicity.
why: It unlocks complex multi-party trades and joint project escrows that today cannot be settled atomically, and identifies which cross-ledger coordination assumptions are genuinely necessary rather than assumed.
key_works: Gomez-Martinez et al. (2024/2025), [Algebraic Zero Knowledge Contingent Payment](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1930).

title: Private recurring condition subscriptions
subfield: Conditional markets, cross-ledger escrow, and auctions
open: Can a user subscribe to a recurring conditional service so that each epoch's data release stays private, while revocation takes effect prospectively — meaning old witnesses neither unlock future releases nor reveal the subscription policy? Formally: construct epoch-specific private subscriptions with prospective revocation, such that historical witnesses cannot be used to open future ciphertexts or to identify the underlying policies.
status: The problem has been proposed as a 1,000×-tier composition target; it is known that revocation cannot recall plaintext already received. Key work: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).
solved_when: A construction meeting the proposed 1,000×-tier composition target exists, realizing epoch-specific private subscriptions with prospective revocation — historical witnesses do not unlock future releases and do not identify policies — with a proof of the claimed guarantees.
why: It would support ongoing conditional data services, where users receive repeated condition-gated releases without each release compromising privacy or future access control.
key_works: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).

title: Durable funding for autonomous research escrow
subfield: Conditional markets, cross-ledger escrow, and auctions
open: Can an escrow design keep funds that back computational proofs auditable and solvent over long horizons, even when multiple valid claims arrive simultaneously? Formally, the question is to maintain verifiable backing for verification or archival expenses across extended durations and concurrent claims without the escrow collapsing.
status: This is currently a proposed funding-design target; existing payment protocols do not make escrow maintenance economically self-sustaining. Related design questions include endowment design, public-goods funding, and escrow solvency. Key work: Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).
solved_when: A funding design exists in which auditable backing for verification and archival expenses remains economically self-sustaining over long horizons, including under simultaneous valid claims.
why: Without it, payment protocols cannot keep long-lived proof incentives solvent and operational, so funded computation breaks down once escrow maintenance costs exceed what the mechanism sustains.
key_works: Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).

title: Complete result-for-payment contracts
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: Can we design a cryptographic contract that binds a payment to an agent's specific task — its executable predicate, its input snapshot, and the delivered artifact — so that verifiable computation and subjective quality are cleanly separated?
status: This is currently a proposed integration target; verifiable computation and contingent service payments are each established components. Key work includes Campanelli et al. (2017), [Zero-Knowledge Contingent Payments Revisited: Attacks and Payments for Services](https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/566).
solved_when: A working contract construction exists that ties payment release to the full bundle of task, executable predicate, input snapshot, and delivered artifact, with verifiable computation handled separately from subjective quality assessment.
why: It would make autonomous procurement precise enough to settle disputes mechanically rather than through trust.
key_works: Campanelli et al. (2017), [Zero-Knowledge Contingent Payments Revisited: Attacks and Payments for Services](https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/566).

title: External-action receipts bound to paid traces
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: Can an agent's proved trace be joined to authenticated evidence about the outside world — verified tool responses, execution identifiers, and the external effects it promised — so that mere assertions by a service are distinguishable from actions that actually occurred?
status: Proposed target; simulated computation alone does not establish a real-world action. Key works: Chiesa–Tromer (2010), [Proof-Carrying Data and Hearsay Arguments from Signature Cards](https://projects.csail.mit.edu/pcd/).
solved_when: A construction exists that binds a proved agent trace to authenticated tool responses and execution identifiers, and clearly separates claimed external effects from verified actual effects.
why: It extends escrow and proof-carrying work beyond isolated computation, so payment and accountability can be tied to real-world actions rather than simulated ones.
key_works: Chiesa–Tromer (2010), [Proof-Carrying Data and Hearsay Arguments from Signature Cards](https://projects.csail.mit.edu/pcd/).

title: Delegation with conserved budgets
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: Can autonomous agents delegate subtasks — along with the authority to spend — to concurrent descendants while still proving that the global budget and scope are conserved end to end? Formally, the question is to design delegation mechanisms whose locally valid proofs compose into a global conservation guarantee across a concurrently spawning tree of agents.
status: The problem is posed as a 1,000×-tier target; the current obstacle is that locally valid proofs do not conserve global resources. Related lines include linear capabilities, concurrent accounting, and resource-aware type systems; a key reference is Chiesa–Tromer (2010), [Proof-Carrying Data and Hearsay Arguments from Signature Cards](https://projects.csail.mit.edu/pcd/).
solved_when: A delegation scheme exists in which agents can spawn concurrent subagents with spending authority, and the scheme produces proofs that global budget and scope are conserved across all descendants — meeting the proposed 1,000×-tier target.
why: It would enable safe subcontracting by AI agents without risk of overspending, turning delegation from a trust assumption into a verifiable guarantee.
key_works: Chiesa–Tromer (2010), [Proof-Carrying Data and Hearsay Arguments from Signature Cards](https://projects.csail.mit.edu/pcd/).

title: Hidden evaluators with enforceable attempt limits
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: Can we build a payment scheme for delegated AI-agent work in which evaluators are committed in advance and kept hidden, so that a solver is paid only for genuinely meeting an arbitrary success predicate — while the scheme enforces a per-identity-resistant budget on evaluation attempts and bounds how much an adaptive solver can learn about the hidden evaluator from repeated queries?
status: Currently only a proposed target; static witness encryption neither limits the number of evaluation attempts nor hides arbitrary predicates. Related lines of work include adaptive data analysis (Dwork et al. (2014/2015), [Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.2664)), Sybil resistance, and benchmark contamination.
solved_when: A construction exists that simultaneously (i) pays only for success against committed hidden evaluators, (ii) enforces attempt limits that resist Sybil-style identity manipulation, and (iii) provably bounds adaptive leakage from repeated evaluation queries.
why: Without it, solvers can game evaluation or repeatedly probe hidden evaluators to reverse-engineer and overfit the success predicate, defeating the purpose of hidden evaluation for proof-carrying work.
key_works: Dwork et al. (2014/2015), [Preserving Statistical Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.2664).

title: Paid stochastic inference without seed cherry-picking
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: Can a randomized inference run be certified so that a paying client knows the output was produced by the committed model, committed inputs, and committed numeric semantics under randomness that was fixed independently of the provider? Formally, this asks for a proof-carrying mechanism that certifies faithful sampling, not merely correct deterministic execution.
status: This is currently a proposed integration target: verifiable neural execution (e.g., Ghodsi et al. (2017), [SafetyNets: Verifiable Execution of Deep Neural Networks on an Untrusted Cloud](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.10268)) does not automatically certify faithful sampling.
solved_when: A construction exists that certifies a paid stochastic inference execution against a committed model, committed inputs, committed numeric semantics, and independently fixed randomness, ruling out post hoc selection of favorable random outcomes.
why: It prevents an untrusted agent from cherry-picking a favorable random outcome after the fact, which is the trust gap left by verifiable neural execution alone.
key_works: Ghodsi et al. (2017), [SafetyNets: Verifiable Execution of Deep Neural Networks on an Untrusted Cloud](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.10268).

title: Proof-triggered scoped tool capabilities
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: Can one release a capability, bound to a specific recipient, that the receiving service can only use subject to enforced constraints on destination, quantity, expiry, and retry count?
status: A 1,000×-tier target has been proposed; currently, disclosed bearer secrets cannot constrain their own subsequent use. Foundational framing traces to Necula (1997), [Proof-Carrying Code](https://doi.org/10.1145/263699.263712).
solved_when: A recipient-bound capability mechanism exists in which destination, quantity, expiry, and retries are all enforced at the receiving service, meeting the proposed 1,000×-tier target.
why: It would turn proofs into narrowly authorized external actions, rather than unrestricted delegations of power.
key_works: Necula (1997), [Proof-Carrying Code](https://doi.org/10.1145/263699.263712).

title: Private attribution of reused agent evidence
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: Can agents reuse previously verified evidence privately, while the system still prevents duplicate payouts for the same artifact and blocks unsupported claims of having discovered it first? Formally, is there a mechanism that lets a prover demonstrate entitled reuse of a verified artifact without revealing it, and without witness possession implying either independent effort or discovery priority?
status: Currently only a proposed target; it is known that witness possession proves neither independent effort nor first discovery. Related to provenance privacy, intellectual attribution, and duplicate detection; see Chiesa–Tromer (2010), [Proof-Carrying Data and Hearsay Arguments from Signature Cards](https://projects.csail.mit.edu/pcd/).
solved_when: A construction (or proof of impossibility) exists in which private reuse of verified artifacts is possible, duplicate payouts are prevented, and no party can claim discovery priority without support — with witness possession alone proving neither independent effort nor first discovery.
why: It would unlock reusable evidence ecosystems for AI agents without indiscriminate reward duplication, letting verified work be shared privately rather than paid out repeatedly.
key_works: Chiesa–Tromer (2010), [Proof-Carrying Data and Hearsay Arguments from Signature Cards](https://projects.csail.mit.edu/pcd/).

title: Fair escrow revision during unfinished work
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: Can an agent's objectives be revised mid-task while its precommitted compensation rights survive intact and completion, cancellation, and stale claims remain verifiable against clear cutoffs? Formally, this asks for a mechanism reconciling mutable objectives with immutable ciphertext policies despite their differing lifecycles.
status: Currently a proposed workflow target; the core tension is that mutable objectives and immutable ciphertext policies have different lifecycles. Related work includes Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740).
solved_when: A revision mechanism exists in which precommitted compensation rights are preserved through objective changes, and verifiable cutoffs distinguish completion, cancellation, and stale claims.
why: It would make long-running autonomous work renegotiable rather than forcing an all-or-nothing choice between abandoning a task and honoring stale terms.
key_works: Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740).

title: Deadlock-free conditional agent workflows
subfield: AI-agent escrow and proof-carrying work
open: When can a cycle of agents — each holding proofs, capabilities, or payments it will release only upon receiving another's — nonetheless be guaranteed to complete fairly? The goal is to characterize the fair completion strategies for such cyclic exchanges and to compile, into executable workflows, exactly the admissible cases under explicit progress assumptions.
status: Proposed as a physics-limit target; the standing observation is that faster verification cannot create a first move in a circular dependency. Related areas include distributed deadlock, session types, and multiparty fairness. Key work: Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740).
solved_when: A characterization of fair completion strategies for cyclic exchanges of proofs, capabilities, and payments exists, together with a compilation procedure for admissible cases that carries explicit progress assumptions.
why: Reliable liveness for large agent production networks: without such a characterization, cyclic dependencies among agents can deadlock, halting cooperative work.
key_works: Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740).

title: Adaptive-compromise security of condition-and-clock hybrids
subfield: Timelock hybrids and temporal conditions
open: Can event witnesses, enforced delays, and threshold beacons be composed into a single release mechanism that remains secure against adversaries who compromise components at different times and exploit correlated component failures? Formally, is there a composition theorem for condition-and-clock hybrids secure under adaptive, temporally staggered compromise?
status: Currently a proposed composition target; only simple AND/OR functionality is available. Key works: Liu et al. (2015/2018), [How to build time-lock encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/482).
solved_when: A composition construction and proof exist that combines event witnesses, delays, and threshold beacons and guarantees security against compromises occurring at different times together with correlated component failures.
why: It would give hybrid release policies an end-to-end lifecycle guarantee, covering not just the release condition itself but the full window in which components may fail or be compromised.
key_works: Liu et al. (2015/2018), [How to build time-lock encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/482).

title: Event-started delays without precomputation
subfield: Timelock hybrids and temporal conditions
open: Can a cryptographic delay be made to begin only once a specific external event has occurred, without any precomputed setup, so that no insider can gain an advantage by anticipating or influencing the event that triggers the challenge? More formally: construct a sequential delay whose start time is bound to a qualifying event, with a provable bound on the advantage of parties who try to predict or manipulate the event.
status: Proposed target only. It is known that VDF sequentiality alone does not establish an external start time. Key work: Boneh et al. (2018), [Verifiable Delay Functions](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/601).
solved_when: A construction (or impossibility result) exists in which the delay starts at the qualifying event with no precomputation phase, and insider advantage from anticipating or influencing the challenge is formally bounded.
why: It enables meaningful "wait this long after the event" policies in timelock hybrid protocols, where the delay must be anchored to an external occurrence rather than to when a computation was initiated.
key_works: Boneh et al. (2018), [Verifiable Delay Functions](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/601).

title: Release deadlines under clock disagreement
subfield: Timelock hybrids and temporal conditions
open: How can a timelock scheme guarantee that a ciphertext opens neither before an earliest time nor after a latest time when the participating systems disagree about what "now" means? Formally, can we compose wall clocks, block timestamps, beacon rounds, and computational-progress proofs into a single release deadline that remains sound when these notions of time diverge?
status: This is a proposed synthesis; existing mechanisms implement different notions of time, and no unified treatment under clock disagreement is known. Key works: Liu et al. (2015/2018), [How to build time-lock encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/482).
solved_when: A construction is given that enforces both an earliest-opening and a latest-opening bound on release, and this guarantee is proved to hold under disagreement among wall clocks, block timestamps, beacon rounds, and computational progress.
why: It makes temporal contracts precise under realistic failures — without it, deadline guarantees in timelock hybrids are ambiguous whenever the underlying time sources diverge.
key_works: Liu et al. (2015/2018), [How to build time-lock encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/482).

title: Weak-client recovery after beacon failure
subfield: Timelock hybrids and temporal conditions
open: When the randomness beacon underpinning a timelock scheme goes dark, can decryption still be made available cheaply to weak clients — without any party being able to open ciphertexts before the intended time — and with a clear designation of who performs and retains the fallback computational work?
status: A 10×-tier resilience target has been proposed; computational-delay and beacon schemes offer different availability properties. Gailly et al. (2023), [tlock: Practical Timelock Encryption from Threshold BLS](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/189).
solved_when: A recovery mechanism achieves the proposed 10×-tier resilience target: inexpensive decryption survives beacon failure, early opening remains impossible, and the performer and holder of fallback work are identified.
why: It keeps low-power recipients from depending permanently on one live service for decryption.
key_works: Gailly et al. (2023), [tlock: Practical Timelock Encryption from Threshold BLS](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/189).

title: Publication-relative proof deadlines
subfield: Timelock hybrids and temporal conditions
open: Can a cryptographic scheme release a secret at the moment a qualifying proof is first publicly committed, rather than at a fixed wall-clock time, while remaining sound against adversaries who withhold witnesses, equivocate on timestamps, or post empty front-running commitments? In other words, is there a construction whose trigger condition is tied to publication of a proof commitment in a way that withstands these manipulation strategies?
status: This is a proposed target with no existing construction. Timestamps, in the tradition of Haber–Stornetta (1991), [How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-38424-3_32), establish publication claims but not when someone first knew a proof — the gap between knowledge and publication that any solution must confront.
solved_when: A construction (or impossibility result) exists for release triggered by the first qualifying public proof commitment, with security argued against withheld witnesses, equivocated timestamps, and empty front-running commitments.
why: It would support defensible priority windows and staged disclosure, grounding release decisions in verifiable publication events rather than unverifiable claims about when someone first knew a proof.
key_works: Haber–Stornetta (1991), [How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-38424-3_32).

title: Optimal future-key continuity through reconfiguration
subfield: Timelock hybrids and temporal conditions
open: What is the minimum amount of honest overlap, handover communication, and retained history needed to keep prepublished ciphertexts decryptable by future committees as membership churns and corruptions move over time — and can a scheme attaining those minima be constructed?
status: Basic continuity is known to exist; the open target is the optimal joint lifecycle cost. Key works: Goyal et al. (2022), [Storing and Retrieving Secrets on a Blockchain](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~bparno/papers/eweb.pdf); Döttling–Hanzlik–Magri–Wohnig (2023/2024), [McFly: Verifiable Encryption to the Future Made Practical](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/433).
solved_when: Tight bounds are established, jointly, for honest overlap, handover communication, and retained history under mobile corruption and committee churn, together with a scheme achieving those optimal values for prepublished ciphertexts.
why: This yields durable encryption to future anonymous committees, so ciphertexts published today remain recoverable across reconfiguration at provably minimal lifecycle cost.
key_works: Goyal et al. (2022), [Storing and Retrieving Secrets on a Blockchain](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~bparno/papers/eweb.pdf); Döttling–Hanzlik–Magri–Wohnig (2023/2024), [McFly: Verifiable Encryption to the Future Made Practical](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/433).

title: Hidden deadlines with public release verification
subfield: Timelock hybrids and temporal conditions
open: Can a timelock scheme hide the release deadline itself while still allowing efficient decryption once it passes and public verification that release occurred correctly, even against adversaries who observe retrieval traffic and test historical witnesses?
