status: The 1,000×-tier target has been proposed but not met; ordinary round timelocks expose their deadlines. Related work includes Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).
solved_when: A construction achieves the 1,000×-tier target for hidden release epochs while retaining efficient decryption, auditability, and resistance to leakage from retrieval patterns and historical-witness testing.
why: It protects private schedules and contingent plans whose timing must remain confidential even after deployment.
key_works: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).

title: Grinding-resistant randomized release
subfield: Timelock hybrids and temporal conditions
open: Can a protocol randomize the release time or recipient of an escrowed message, using committed external entropy, in a way that no party can bias through ciphertext grinding, selective nonpublication, or correlated escrows? Formally, the question is to construct (or rule out) schemes where the distribution over published escrows matches the beacon's distribution even when the publishing party is adversarial.
status: Currently a proposed target only. It is known that valid randomness beacons alone do not suffice, since they do not prevent a biased selection of which escrow to publish. Key work: Boneh et al. (2018), [Verifiable Delay Functions](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/601).
solved_when: A construction is given for randomized release times or recipients derived from committed external entropy, with provable resistance to ciphertext grinding, selective nonpublication, and correlated escrows; or an impossibility result is established.
why: It would make randomized allocation and disclosure rules credible — parties could trust that the randomness actually governing release, not just the beacon output, has not been manipulated.
key_works: Boneh et al. (2018), [Verifiable Delay Functions](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/601).

title: Authorized vulnerability-proof payment
subfield: Verifiable vulnerability bounties and confidential repair
open: Can a protocol pay out a bounty for a zero-knowledge proof that a real security violation exists within an authorized test artifact, while cryptographically binding the reward, the agreed scope, and the delivered remediation evidence?
status: Proposed integration target only; zero-knowledge vulnerability proofs and contingent payment mechanisms exist separately but have not been combined. Key work: Cuéllar et al. (2023), [Cheesecloth: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Real World Vulnerabilities](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity23/presentation/cuellar).
solved_when: A working integration exists in which a vulnerability proof in scope triggers a contingent payment, with reward, scope, and remediation evidence all bound in a single verifiable flow.
why: It rewards defensive discovery without forcing premature public disclosure, closing the gap between finding a bug and safely getting it fixed and paid.
key_works: Cuéllar et al. (2023), [Cheesecloth: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Real World Vulnerabilities](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity23/presentation/cuellar).

title: Severity certificates beyond reachability
subfield: Verifiable vulnerability bounties and confidential repair
open: Can we define private certificates that distinguish a committed security-boundary violation from merely unusual but irrelevant program states, and measure how well such certificates agree with independent expert judgments of severity?
status: This is a proposed experimental target; currently, trace validity alone does not establish operational severity. Key works: Green et al. (2022/2023), [Efficient Proofs of Software Exploitability for Real-world Processors](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1223).
solved_when: A certificate definition exists that separates genuine security-boundary violations from irrelevant unusual states, and an experimental evaluation demonstrates measurable agreement with independent expert severity judgments.
why: It makes automated bounty prices correspond to meaningful defects rather than to traces that are merely valid.
key_works: Green et al. (2022/2023), [Efficient Proofs of Software Exploitability for Real-world Processors](https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/1223).

title: Private duplicate-vulnerability adjudication
subfield: Verifiable vulnerability bounties and confidential repair
open: Can duplicate confidential vulnerability reports be identified without revealing their contents, so that only genuinely independent discoveries are rewarded separately? A satisfactory answer needs a bounded, measurable notion of report equivalence that distinguishes true duplicates from mere trace variations of the same defect.
status: Proposed as a data-and-protocol target; it is noted that unequal proofs need not represent distinct defects. Related areas include semantic clone detection, private set intersection, and defect taxonomy, with Cuéllar et al. (2023), [Cheesecloth: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Real World Vulnerabilities](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity23/presentation/cuellar), as a key work.
solved_when: A protocol exists that adjudicates duplicate claims on confidential reports without revealing them, under a bounded equivalence definition with quantified, measured error rates.
why: It preserves bounty budgets from being drained by trace variations, and rewards independent discoveries fairly.
key_works: Cuéllar et al. (2023), [Cheesecloth: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Real World Vulnerabilities](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity23/presentation/cuellar).

title: Patch-conditioned confidential disclosure
subfield: Verifiable vulnerability bounties and confidential repair
open: Can we build a disclosure mechanism that releases vulnerability evidence only to designated audiences, triggered either by a committed patch certificate or an elapsed deadline — and that rejects so-called fixes which merely stop one specific demonstration without establishing the promised property?
status: This is currently a proposed 10×-tier target; the key observation motivating it is that stopping one demonstration does not certify a repair. Related to Luick et al. (2024), [ZKSMT: A VM for Proving SMT Theorems in Zero Knowledge](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/luick).
solved_when: A working system achieves release of evidence to designated audiences upon committed patch certificates or deadlines, while provably rejecting example-specific fixes that fail the promised property (the proposed 10×-tier target).
why: It ties disclosure incentives to verified remediation, so bounties reward genuine repairs rather than patches that merely suppress a single exploit demonstration.
key_works: Luick et al. (2024), [ZKSMT: A VM for Proving SMT Theorems in Zero Knowledge](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/luick).

title: Private proof of repair coverage
subfield: Verifiable vulnerability bounties and confidential repair
open: Can a repairer prove in zero knowledge that a fix eliminates an entire committed class of violations, while the repaired artifact still provides its specified functionality and is actually delivered? Formally: construct a proof system (or scheme) attesting universal removal of a violation class over the artifact, without revealing the fix itself.
status: Proposed target; no construction is known. Luick et al. (2024), [ZKSMT: A VM for Proving SMT Theorems in Zero Knowledge](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/luick) is the cited key work; related areas include relational verification, patch correctness, and proof-carrying software.
solved_when: A scheme exists that proves, for a committed violation class, that no instance of that class remains, preserves the specified functionality of the artifact, and delivers the proved artifact — with finite tests clearly not presented as universal correctness.
why: It enables repair markets and bounties that pay for eliminating whole classes of defects rather than single demonstrated fixes, while keeping the repair confidential.
key_works: Luick et al. (2024), [ZKSMT: A VM for Proving SMT Theorems in Zero Knowledge](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity24/presentation/luick).

title: Evidence preservation through long disclosure windows
subfield: Verifiable vulnerability bounties and confidential repair
open: Can confidential vulnerability reports, their proofs, verifiers, and authorized recovery paths be kept usable across long remediation windows — surviving personnel changes — without creating new disclosure bypasses? Formally, this asks for an engineering design that preserves not just encrypted bytes but the execution environments and provenance needed to later verify and act on the evidence.
status: Currently a proposed archival target. It is recognized that execution environments and provenance need preservation alongside encrypted bytes; no implementation exists yet. Related areas include reproducible environments and digital evidence preservation. Key work: Goyal et al. (2022), [Storing and Retrieving Secrets on a Blockchain](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~bparno/papers/eweb.pdf).
solved_when: A working system preserves confidential reports, proofs, verifiers, and authorized recovery across long remediation windows and personnel changes, with execution environments and provenance preserved alongside the encrypted data, and no disclosure bypass introduced.
why: It keeps long-window evidence usable for verification and repair even as staff turn over, while preventing the preservation mechanism itself from becoming a leak channel.
key_works: Goyal et al. (2022), [Storing and Retrieving Secrets on a Blockchain](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~bparno/papers/eweb.pdf).

title: Sponsored discovery without budget exhaustion
subfield: Verifiable vulnerability bounties and confidential repair
open: How can a vulnerability-bounty program allocate rewards when it faces a flood of valid but low-value or overlapping claims, while still preserving private screening, Sybil resistance, and open access for honest researchers? In formal terms, this asks for a mechanism that remains budget-sound under adversarial claim floods without sacrificing confidentiality of screening or permissionless participation.
status: A 1,000×-tier mechanism has been proposed; however, proof correctness alone does not determine the economic value of a claim, leaving the allocation problem open. Background: Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).
solved_when: A mechanism is given that provably prevents budget exhaustion (as targeted by the proposed 1,000×-tier design) under floods of valid low-value or overlapping claims, while simultaneously achieving private screening, Sybil resistance, and open researcher access.
why: A solution keeps automated defensive programs financially sustainable; without it, adversarial floods of cheap valid claims can drain the bounty budget and shut the program down.
key_works: Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).

title: Verifier-failure contingency for defensive escrow
subfield: Verifiable vulnerability bounties and confidential repair
open: Can a defensive escrow system be equipped with a precommitted recovery procedure that activates when a verifier or compiler is later shown to be unsound, so that already-settled claims and still-pending claims are handled differently while fabricated failure allegations gain nothing?
status: Currently only a proposed lifecycle target; recovery cannot retract already disclosed secrets. Related to emergency protocol governance and verifiable incident response. Key work: Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740).
solved_when: A recovery mechanism exists that, upon demonstrated verifier or compiler unsoundness, distinguishes settled from pending claims and resists fabricated failure allegations, with the caveat that it cannot retract already disclosed secrets.
why: It gives long-lived bounty systems an accountable failure path instead of leaving them without recourse when the underlying verification infrastructure breaks.
key_works: Dziembowski et al. (2018), [FairSwap: How to fairly exchange digital goods](https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/740).

title: Reproduction-gated scientific data release
subfield: Scientific release, consent, archives, and optimization
open: Can scientific data artifacts be released automatically only once it is verifiably established that the declared computations were actually carried out on authenticated inputs? In other words, can a system unlock artifacts when certificates verify those computations, under precise provenance and acceptance rules?
status: The proposal sets a 10×-tier target; it is noted that computational reproduction does not certify truthful physical measurement. Key work: Gennaro et al. (2010), [Non-Interactive Verifiable Computing: Outsourcing Computation to Untrusted Workers](https://eprint.iacr.org/2009/547).
solved_when: A working system exists in which artifacts unlock only after certificates verify the declared computations on authenticated inputs, with precise provenance and acceptance rules specified; the proposed 10×-tier target serves as the quantitative benchmark.
why: It ties data access to demonstrably reproducible scientific work, making release contingent on verified computation rather than trust.
key_works: Gennaro et al. (2010), [Non-Interactive Verifiable Computing: Outsourcing Computation to Untrusted Workers](https://eprint.iacr.org/2009/547).

title: Independently replicated-result thresholds
subfield: Scientific release, consent, archives, and optimization
open: When should a system release funds or data on the strength of replication certificates, if the replications may not be truly independent? The goal is a release mechanism that operates under a defensible independence model, explicitly quantifying correlations arising from shared methods and shared data among the replicating experiments.
status: Currently a proposed experimental target; it is noted that threshold credentials do not establish that experiments are independent. Related work includes Zhang et al. (2016), [Town Crier: An Authenticated Data Feed for Smart Contracts](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/168).
solved_when: A release rule is specified that, given replication certificates, decides release under an independence model with explicit quantification of shared-method and shared-data correlations, and its behavior is validated experimentally against correlated replications.
why: Without such a model, correlated replications can masquerade as independent confirmation and create false confidence in a result, leading to premature release of funds or data.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2016), [Town Crier: An Authenticated Data Feed for Smart Contracts](https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/168).

title: Preregistered release without selective omission
subfield: Scientific release, consent, archives, and optimization
open: Can a release process be designed so that analysts commit to their complete analysis and publication plans before seeing outcomes, and so that it is publicly verifiable afterward that every required result was actually released, including unfavorable ones?
status: Currently only a proposed target. Existing primitives such as timestamps and execution proofs, each taken separately, do not establish that complete publication occurred; related ideas include Haber–Stornetta (1991), [How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-38424-3_32).
solved_when: A mechanism exists in which commitments to the full analysis and release plan are made before outcomes are observed, and a verifier can prove that every required result in the plan was included in the release, with no channel for selective omission.
why: It prevents conditional-release infrastructure from reinforcing publication bias, ensuring that preregistration cannot be undermined by quietly dropping results.
key_works: Haber–Stornetta (1991), [How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-38424-3_32).

title: Statistically valid adaptive release conditions
subfield: Scientific release, consent, archives, and optimization
open: Can we guarantee that a system releasing automated evidence only when a statistical test passes controls its false-release probability even when tests are run repeatedly, stopped at data-dependent times, and chosen adaptively? Formally, this asks for anytime-valid release conditions that bind the testing procedure and the full access history to the released witness, so validity survives optional stopping and adaptive hypothesis selection.
status: The problem is stated as a 1,000×-tier target with no solution yet. The natural toolkit is anytime-valid inference and adaptive data analysis, in the spirit of Howard et al. (2021), [Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08240).
solved_when: A release condition is given with a proven anytime-valid bound on false-release probability under repeated testing, optional stopping, and adaptive hypothesis selection, with the procedure and access history cryptographically or structurally bound to the witness, and the bound holds at the record's 1,000×-tier target.
why: Verified computation alone cannot repair invalid statistical inference, so without such conditions automated evidence thresholds are scientifically indefensible; with them, they become defensible.
key_works: Howard et al. (2021), [Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08240).

title: Consent-scoped release with prospective withdrawal
subfield: Scientific release, consent, archives, and optimization
open: Can we release data records so that only those whose authenticated consent explicitly permits a given recipient and computation at a finalized epoch become decryptable, while all unrelated policies and identities remain hidden? In other words, can a release be made consent-scoped and prospective-withdrawable, where access is decided by the consent state at the epoch of release?
status: This is a proposed engineering target; no construction is known. Withdrawal is prospective only — it governs future access and cannot recall plaintext already released. Related primitives appear in Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).
solved_when: A construction exists that releases only records whose authenticated consent permits the specified recipients and computations at finalized epochs, hides unrelated policies and identities, and enforces withdrawal prospectively — i.e., withdrawal blocks all future access, with no requirement to recall plaintext already released.
why: It would enable precise, policy-faithful conditional access to sensitive datasets, letting archives honor per-recipient and per-computation consent without leaking which other policies or identities are involved.
key_works: Faust et al. (2023), [Statement-Oblivious Threshold Witness Encryption](https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/668).

title: Training-data access with verifiable usage receipts
subfield: Scientific release, consent, archives, and optimization
open: Can a data holder grant access to training data only for authorized computations, in a way that provably separates what was actually executed from any promises about retained plaintext or models trained later? In other words, can verifiable execution guarantees be made orthogonal to — and explicitly weaker than — confinement guarantees about what the recipient keeps afterward?
status: Currently a physics-limit target: downstream confinement is known to require hardware, MPC, or service assumptions beyond witness encryption. Verifiable outsourcing techniques such as Gennaro et al. (2010), [Non-Interactive Verifiable Computing: Outsourcing Computation to Untrusted Workers](https://eprint.iacr.org/2009/547), address the execution-proof side but not retention.
solved_when: A construction exists that (i) verifiably restricts access to authorized computations, and (ii) formally distinguishes proven execution from unproven claims about retained plaintext or subsequently trained models, with the residual confinement gap made explicit and delegated to hardware, MPC, or service assumptions.
why: It would turn data-use agreements from legal text into technically enforceable, checkable terms, which is what consent-based archives and scientific data release actually need.
key_works: Gennaro et al. (2010), [Non-Interactive Verifiable Computing: Outsourcing Computation to Untrusted Workers](https://eprint.iacr.org/2009/547).

title: Self-describing conditional archives
subfield: Scientific release, consent, archives, and optimization
open: Can an archive of conditionally encrypted knowledge carry enough embedded, executable and mathematical specification that future parties — with no out-of-band context — can reimplement release verifiers and check consistency with the stored ciphertexts and migration certificates?
status: A 10×-tier archival target has been proposed, but surviving bytes and timestamps alone are currently considered insufficient to meet it.
solved_when: An archival package meeting the proposed 10×-tier archival target contains sufficient executable and mathematical specification to reimplement release verifiers and verify consistency with ciphertexts and migration certificates, going beyond mere surviving bytes and timestamps.
why: Without embedded specification, conditionally encrypted knowledge becomes uninterpretable across generations; with it, future verifiers can be rebuilt from the archive itself.
key_works: Haber–Stornetta (1991), [How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-38424-3_32).

title: Optimization-certificate reward ladders
subfield: Scientific release, consent, archives, and optimization
open: Can we design a reward structure that pays for genuinely improved feasible solutions and certified bounds in hard optimization problems, while making it impossible to cash in repeatedly on essentially the same claim — all using certificate classes that remain tractable to verify?
status: The problem proposes a 1,000×-tier target; it is noted that faster WE does not make every global-optimality claim NP-verifiable. Key work: Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).
solved_when: A reward ladder is specified in which each payout tier requires a certificate of improvement from a tractable class, equivalent repeat claims are provably excluded, and the proposal's 1,000×-tier target is met or the target is shown unachievable; the construction must also respect the fact that faster witness encryption does not make every global-optimality claim NP-verifiable.
why: It converts optimization progress into a continuously incentivized, measurable activity, rewarding each genuine improvement rather than a single winner-take-all solution.
key_works: Kumaresan–Bentov (2014), [How to Use Bitcoin to Incentivize Correct Computations](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-bitcoin-incentivize-correct-computations/).
